fiches.corps:
::A bow is a stick you learn to bend without breaking it. The whole craft fits in that sentence, and in the patience it takes.::

## UNDERSTAND

When you draw the string, the back of the bow (the side facing the target) **stretches** and the belly (the side facing you) **compresses**. A bow almost always breaks for one of two reasons: a cut fibre on the back that fails under tension, or a thin spot on the belly that crushes and wrinkles.

Hence the two rules that govern everything else:

**Leave the back alone.** It must follow a single growth ring from one end to the other. Remove the bark, nothing more.

**All the work is done on the belly**, in small passes, checking constantly that both limbs bend the same. This is called **tillering**.

A decent bow takes a few days of work and dry wood. If you have neither, start with the sling and the spear in [[SURV-ARM-002]].

## ACT

### 1. Find the wood

**The best**: yew, elm, ash, maple, black locust, hazel, dogwood, white oak, hickory. What matters is not the species but **straight grain**.

**A trunk or branch** 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 in) across, straight over 1.80 m (6 ft), with no knots or twist. Split it in half or in quarters with wedges: the split follows the fibres and gives you an intact back.

**In a town**, a board from a hardware store makes a very good bow if the grain runs from end to end without running off the sides. Look at the edges: the lines must be parallel all the way. This is the "board bow", the quickest to make.

### 2. Dry it

Green wood bends but doesn't spring back. Debark it, seal the ends (glue, wax, paint) to stop cracks, and store it sheltered and dry, **never near a fire**.

To save time: rough the bow out to three quarters **while it's green**, then let that thin shape dry. Two to four weeks is then enough, instead of months for a whole quarter log.

### 3. Lay it out

For a straight flat bow, easy and forgiving:

- **Length**: 1.70 to 1.80 m (5 ft 7 in to 6 ft), roughly your height.
- **Handle** in the centre, 10 cm (4 in), left unworked.
- **Width**: 4 to 5 cm (1.6 to 2 in) where the limbs start, tapering in a straight line to 1.2 cm (1/2 in) at the tips.
- **Thickness**: around 2 cm near the handle, 1 cm at the tips, removing wood from the belly only.

Draw the outline in pencil on the back, cut with a hatchet or knife, finish with a rasp or drawknife. Stop short of the final dimensions: tillering will do the rest.

### 4. Tillering

This is the step that makes or breaks the bow.

1. Cut two shallow **nocks** at each tip, on the sides, without touching the back.
2. Fit a **long string**, longer than the bow, that barely bends it.
3. Fix a **tillering stick** to the wall: a board with notches every 5 cm (2 in). Rest the handle on top, pull the string to the first notch.
4. Step back and **look**. The two limbs must form two smooth, symmetrical curves. A spot that stays straight is too thick: scrape it, on the belly. A spot that bends more than the rest is too thin: don't touch it again, work around it.
5. Go down one notch. Start again. **Dozens of times.**

Never pull further than the length you will actually draw, and never hold the bow drawn for long: every extra second tires it.

When the bow bends nicely at half draw, fit the real string: the distance between string and handle (the **brace height**) should be about **15 cm (6 in)**, a fist with the thumb raised. Keep tillering up to your full draw length.

### 5. The string

A good string must be stronger than the bow needs, and must not stretch.

- **Salvaged synthetic**: paracord inner strands, braided nylon thread, braided fishing line, in several strands.
- **Natural**: flax, hemp, nettle, sinew, in a two-ply Flemish twist. See [[TEC-MAT-003]].

A loop at one end, a bowyer's knot at the other, which lets you adjust the length.

### 6. The arrows

**They matter more than the bow.** A good bow with bad arrows hits nothing.

- **Shaft**: straight shoots of hazel, dogwood, viburnum, cane, or hardware-store dowel. Diameter 8 to 9 mm (5/16 to 11/32 in). Straighten them by warming gently over embers and bending by hand.
- **Length**: your draw length plus 3 to 5 cm (1 to 2 in). Measure draw length with the arm stretched out, from the hollow of the throat to the fingertips.
- **Nock** at the back, sawn or carved, in line with the grain.
- **Fletching**: three half feathers from the same wing, glued and bound, at 120 degrees.
- **Point**: a flattened nail, sheet metal, bone, knapped stone, or simply fire-hardened wood for small game.

Make them **all alike**: same length, same weight, same stiffness. Weigh them, sort them.

### 7. Finish

Sand, round the edges of the back (a sharp edge concentrates stress), grease or wax the wood against damp. **Unstring the bow after every session**: left strung, it takes a permanent bend and loses power.

## ADAPT

**You only have a PVC pipe.** A 2 cm (3/4 in) pipe heated and flattened at the ends makes a practice bow in an hour. It is weak and ages badly, but it teaches the movement.

**Your bow breaks.** Damaged back, wood not dry enough, or a spot that bent too much and went unnoticed during tillering. Start again with wider, thinner wood: a wide flat bow forgives almost everything.

**Your bow is too stiff.** Scrape the belly of both limbs evenly, then redo a full tillering. **Too weak**: shortening a few centimetres at both tips makes it stiffer.

**You want to hunt.** You need at least 18 to 20 kg (40 to 45 lb) of draw weight at your draw length, heavy arrows and a sharp point. Shoot at under 20 m (22 yd), at a still animal, and first learn to group on a target. See [[TEC-MEC-008]] and [[SURV-RES-002]].

**Is the bow legal?** In France, bows are freely sold, but bowhunting requires a hunting licence and specific training. Rules differ by country. Shoot only where an arrow cannot leave the ground.

fiches.corps:
::A bow throws nothing. It stores the strength of your arms for two seconds, then gives it back in a hundredth of a second. Everything else follows from that.::

## What happens when you shoot

Drawing the string bends the limbs: they store your effort like a spring. When your fingers open, they spring back, the string pushes the arrow, and the energy turns into motion.

Not all of it goes into the arrow. Part stays in the limbs and string, which keep moving and vibrating: that is the noise and the jolt in your hand. **A wooden longbow returns about 70% of the energy stored**, a modern bow a bit more.

In numbers, for a simple hunting bow: a 25 g arrow leaving at 55 m/s (180 ft/s) carries about **38 joules**. That's a thousand times less than a rifle bullet, see [[TEC-BAL-001]], but plenty to pass through game at short range when the point cuts.

**Arrow weight matters.** A light arrow leaves faster; a heavy one takes a larger share of the energy, and hits harder. Dry firing, shooting without an arrow, is the mistake that breaks bows: all the energy stays in the wood.

## The three families of bows

**The longbow**: one piece, the limbs bend evenly. Simple, quiet, makeable, see [[SURV-ARM-005]].

**The recurve**: the tips curve forward. They unroll as you draw, which stores more energy for the same length and gives a faster arrow. It's the Olympic bow.

**The compound**: cams at the ends change the leverage during the draw. **The hardest part is mid-draw, then the force drops by 65 to 85%** at full draw. You can aim for a long time without shaking. In return, it is heavy, mechanical and hard to repair far from a workshop.

## The archer's paradox

On a simple bow, the arrow rests beside the wood, not in the centre. Yet it flies straight. The reason: at release, the arrow **flexes** into an S under the push of the string, bends around the handle, then straightens in flight.

That is why the arrow's stiffness (its **spine**) must match the bow's power. Too flexible, it flies left (for a right-hander); too stiff, it flies right. **Half of all bad shots come from mismatched arrows**, not from the archer.

## Shooting: the movement

A shot is always built in the same order. Consistency matters more than strength.

1. **Stance**: side-on, feet shoulder-width apart, square to the target.
2. **Nock**: arrow on the rest, nock on the string, the coloured feather facing out.
3. **Fingers**: three fingers on the string, index above the arrow, the other two below, the string in the crease of the first joint.
4. **Raise and draw**: bow arm straight but not locked, elbow turned slightly out. Draw with **your back**, bringing the shoulder blades together, not with the biceps.
5. **Anchor**: the string hand always comes to the same spot on the face, under the jaw or at the corner of the mouth. That's what makes every shot identical.
6. **Aim**: dominant eye above the arrow. To find your dominant eye, frame a distant point in a circle made with both hands, then close one eye: the one that still sees the point is the right one.
7. **Release**: relax the fingers, don't open the hand. The string hand slides back along the neck by itself.
8. **Hold**: stay in position until the arrow lands. Moving at release throws the shot off.

## Getting better

Start at **5 metres** (5 yd), on a big target, with a light bow. The aim is not to hit the centre but to **group**: to land the arrows together. A tight group in the wrong place is fixed by aiming elsewhere; a scattered one is not.

Step back once your arrows group. A trained archer puts arrows inside a hand at 20 m (22 yd) with a simple bow. Beyond 30 m, the trajectory curves steeply and judging distance becomes the real problem.

## Safety

- Nobody in front of the shooting line, ever.
- Behind the target: a bank, a mound or a net. A missed arrow can fly more than 100 m (110 yd).
- Check every arrow: a cracked arrow can shatter at release and go through your hand.
- **Never dry fire.**
- A leather finger tab and an arm guard prevent blisters and bruised wrists.

fiches.corps:
::A bank card holds no money. It holds a key that proves it's really that card. The terminal pays nothing: it asks the bank a question, and waits for the answer.::

## What's in the card

The chip is a real little computer, with protected memory. It keeps a **secret key** that it never reveals, even to whoever reads it. For each payment, it uses it to compute a **cryptogram**: a unique code, valid for this transaction, this amount, this day.

That's what makes a chip card hard to copy. You can read its number, not its key; and a stolen cryptogram works only once.

**The magnetic stripe** on the back holds only the number and the expiry date. It's easy to copy: that's why it's hardly used in Europe any more.

## What happens in two seconds

1. **Reading.** The terminal talks to the chip, by contact or by radio.
2. **The PIN.** You type your PIN. In Europe, most of the time **the chip itself checks it**: the PIN never goes to the bank. Three mistakes and it locks.
3. **The request.** The terminal sends the amount and the cryptogram to the merchant's bank (the **acquirer**).
4. **The network.** The acquirer passes it through the card's network (CB, Visa, Mastercard) to **your bank**, the issuer.
5. **The decision.** Your bank checks the cryptogram, the balance or limit, signs of fraud, and answers yes or no.
6. **The receipt.** The answer comes back the same way. All of this takes one to three seconds.

**The money itself doesn't move yet.** In the evening, the terminal sends all the day's transactions in one batch. The banks settle between themselves, and the merchant is credited a day or two later, minus a fee.

## Contactless

The card contains a small antenna. The terminal emits a radio field at **13.56 MHz** that powers the chip from a few centimetres away, with no battery. Payment terminals are designed to read at under about 4 cm (1.5 in).

To go fast, the PIN is skipped below a set amount, **50 euros in France** (the limit varies by country). To limit risk if the card is stolen, it counts payments made without a PIN: past a cumulative amount or a number of transactions, it asks for the PIN on the next payment.

**A phone** works the same way, but the card number is replaced by a substitute number, and your fingerprint or face replaces the PIN.

## Why it can say no

- Spending limit reached (often over a rolling 7 or 30 days).
- Card blocked, expired, or worn chip: try contactless, or the other way round.
- Suspected fraud: unusual purchase, unusual country. Your banking app often flags it.
- **No network.**

## When the network goes down

A terminal needs two things: **power and a link** (landline, internet, or a SIM card for mobile terminals).

Some terminals can accept a payment **offline** under a small amount set by the bank (the floor limit): the chip checks the PIN and the card alone, the transaction is stored and sent later. It's a risk for the merchant, who limits or refuses it.

During a wide blackout, like in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025, terminals stop along with everything else: shops still open accept **cash only**. Keep some at home, in small notes. See [[TEC-RES-001]].

## Protecting yourself

- **Cover the keypad** when typing your PIN: a camera or a glance is enough to steal it, and the card gets stolen next.
- **Look at the terminal** of a cash machine or a petrol pump: a front that moves, a thick reader, a raised keypad can hide a skimmer.
- **The amount shown** is the one you agree to: read it before presenting the card.
- **A lost card** must be cancelled immediately, through the app or your bank's number. In France, the interbank card cancellation number is 0 892 705 705.
- A stolen contactless card is limited by its counter; online payment with your numbers is the real risk. Watch your statements.

fiches.corps:
::A street camera is almost never watched live. It is mostly used afterwards, provided someone asks for the footage in time.::

## How a city network works

A town's cameras are linked by fibre or radio to a **control room**: a room, a wall of screens, a few operators. French law calls cameras on public streets **vidéoprotection**, and those in private places vidéosurveillance.

An operator can only really follow a few screens at once. In a city with hundreds of cameras, **the vast majority of footage is seen by no one**. It is recorded, then erased.

Three uses dominate:

- **Live**: following a demonstration, a match, an incident reported by radio.
- **Afterwards**: police or courts request footage of a precise place and time. This is by far the main use.
- **Plate reading** (ANPR): dedicated cameras read number plates and compare them to lists of wanted vehicles.

How a camera works technically is covered in [[TEC-IDE-004]].

## What the law says in France

- Every camera on a public street needs **authorisation from the prefect**, after the opinion of a local commission.
- It must not film inside homes, nor their entrances in detail.
- **Signs** must mark the filmed area and say whom to contact.
- Footage is kept **30 days at most**, often less. Then it is erased, unless an investigation has requested it.
- Anyone can ask to see footage in which they appear, from the person named on the sign. Refusal is possible for security or investigation reasons; it can be challenged before the local commission.

Other countries have their own rules; in the UK, for instance, requests go through a subject access request under data protection law.

**Live facial recognition in the street is not allowed in France.** At European level, the 2024 AI regulation forbids it to law enforcement, except for narrow cases (searching for a victim, an imminent terrorist threat) supervised by a judge.

**Automated video analysis**, without face recognition, was trialled for the 2024 Olympics: spotting an abandoned object, a crowd surge, a person on the ground. Its future is the subject of debates and successive laws: check the law as it stands when you read this.

## Does it work?

The most solid answer comes from an analysis of 76 studies carried out over forty years (Piza and colleagues, 2019):

- a **modest drop** in crime where the cameras are, around 13% on average;
- a clear effect on **car parks** and vehicle-related theft;
- **no measurable effect on violence**: nobody thinks about the camera in the middle of a fight.

In France, the Court of Audit noted in 2020 that no overall link had been established between how many cameras a city has and its crime level. A study commissioned by the gendarmerie in 2021 found that footage had contributed to only a small fraction of solved investigations.

What cameras do well: **retrace a route afterwards**, confirm a time, find a vehicle. What they do badly: prevent.

## What's actually useful to you

**You are a victim or a witness.** Report it **within days**, giving the exact place and time. The complaint is what lets the police request the footage before it is erased. After a month, it no longer exists. Note the shops nearby too: their private cameras often have a better view than the city's.

**You want to know where the cameras are.** Signs, town council minutes (installation is voted and funded in public), some cities' open data, and collaborative maps like OpenStreetMap, where volunteers log cameras.

**You want to see your footage.** Write to the person named on the sign, within the retention period, giving place, date, time and a description of yourself.

**You care about your privacy.** A street camera is one link among many; your phone, your payments and your badges say far more. See [[SIG-COM-007]].

**During a long blackout.** A camera network depends on power and links. Without them, it goes dark like everything else, see [[TEC-RES-001]].

fiches.corps:
::A camera doesn't see better than you. It sees longer, without blinking, and it keeps everything. That's its only strength, and its weaknesses come from the same place.::

## What's inside

A security camera is a camera that takes 15 to 30 pictures a second, non-stop.

**The lens** gathers light. Its focal length decides everything: short, it sees wide but details are small; long, it sees far but narrow. A camera cannot see everything in detail at once.

**The sensor** turns light into pixels. More pixels let you zoom into the image, but only if the lens and the light keep up.

**The infrared filter.** By day, a small filter blocks infrared to keep colours right. At night, it slides away with a little click, the camera switches to black and white and lights the scene itself with **infrared LEDs**.

**The processor** compresses the image and sends it. It often also handles motion detection, sometimes recognition of people or vehicles.

## Night vision

Infrared LEDs at **850 nm** give off a dull red glow, visible to the eye when you look at the camera in the dark. Those at **940 nm** are invisible, but reach less far.

This lighting has a limited range, often 20 to 30 m (65 to 100 ft). Beyond it, the image is black. See [[TEC-NUI-001]] for night vision in general.

**A phone camera sees infrared**: film the camera in the dark, its LEDs show up as purple or white dots.

## Analogue or IP

**Analogue cameras** (and their modern HD versions over coaxial cable) send a raw video signal to a recorder, the **DVR**. Everything stays in the building.

**IP cameras** are small computers on the network. They send a digital stream to a network recorder (**NVR**), a server or a cloud. Many are powered by the network cable itself (**PoE**, Power over Ethernet).

**Consumer WiFi cameras** almost always send their footage to the maker's servers. Without internet, many do nothing more, or only record to their memory card.

## Why compression matters

Raw video would fill a disk in a few hours. The **H.264** and **H.265** codecs keep only what changes from one frame to the next. An empty car park costs almost nothing; a street in the rain or a tree in the wind costs a lot, because everything moves.

In practice, a recorder often keeps **one to four weeks**, then overwrites the oldest footage. **If you need a recording, ask for it quickly.**

## Detect, recognise, identify

The European standard EN 62676-4 sets what you can expect from an image according to how many pixels cover one metre of the scene:

| Goal | Pixels per metre | What you can tell |
|---|---|---|
| Detect | 25 | Someone is there |
| Observe | 62 | What they're doing, their clothes |
| Recognise | 125 | It's someone you know |
| Identify | 250 | You can establish who it is |

A 4K camera covering a 40 m (130 ft) wide car park gives about 100 pixels per metre: it may recognise, it doesn't identify. **That's why footage on the TV news is so blurry.**

## What fools a camera

- **Backlight**: a figure in front of a glass door or headlights turns black. So-called WDR cameras partly compensate.
- **Window reflections**: a camera behind a window, at night, sees only the reflection of its own LEDs.
- **Rain, snow, spider webs** in front of the lens trigger motion detection endlessly, or blind the image at night.
- **Angle**: a camera mounted too high sees only the tops of heads and cap peaks.
- **The network**: a poorly protected IP camera, with its factory password, can be reached from the internet. Entire websites list open cameras.

## Installing your own

1. Decide **what you want to see**: the entrance, a driveway, a letterbox. One camera per need, not one camera for everything.
2. Mount it **2.5 to 3 m (8 to 10 ft) high**, low enough to see faces, high enough not to be torn down.
3. Avoid backlight: not facing east or west, not facing a lamp.
4. **Change the password** at install, update it, and if possible keep it on a separate network.
5. Prefer **local** recording (card, NVR): it works without internet.

**The law.** In France, an individual may only film their own property. The public street, the garden or the neighbours' windows are off limits. Employees must be informed, and footage may not be kept more than a month. Rules differ by country. City cameras follow other rules, see [[TEC-IDE-005]].

fiches.corps:
::A stone feeds no one. A shoe, hardly. But both soups tell something true: one about hunger, the other about what people give each other when they're given the chance.::

## UNDERSTAND

### The tale

A hungry traveller arrives in a village. Nobody will give him anything. He sets a pot of water on the fire, drops in a well-washed stone, and announces he's making a delicious soup. The villagers, curious, come closer. "It would be better with an onion," he says. Someone brings one. Then a carrot, a piece of bacon, salt, potatoes. In the end, the whole village eats a real soup. The stone gave nothing.

The tale exists all over Europe, with a nail, a button or an axe instead of the stone.

### What's true in it

**The stone doesn't feed.** It brings no calories. At most, a limestone pebble releases a few minerals into an acidic broth.

**But the mechanism is real.** Everyone has a little, nobody has enough, and nobody wants to be the first to give. It takes one person to set the pot down and make sharing easy, visible and joyful. Crisis kitchens, soup kitchens and street meals after a disaster work exactly like this. See [[SURV-SOC-001]].

### Shoe soup

The image comes from the cinema: in The Gold Rush (1925), Charlie Chaplin's prospector, starving and snowed into a cabin, boils his shoe and eats it like a roast, with the laces as spaghetti.

Reality came before the film:

- **The Donner Party**, trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in 1846, boiled ox hides to get a jelly out of them.
- **During the siege of Leningrad** (1941 to 1944), people boiled belts, bags and leather book bindings, and scraped off wallpaper paste, which was made of flour.
- Sailors, encircled soldiers and polar explorers ate their harnesses and their boots.

### What leather is really worth

Leather is skin, so mostly **collagen**: a protein. Boiled for a long time, raw hide gives a jelly, like the gelatin from a pig's trotter. So there is a little food in it.

**But:**

- collagen is an incomplete protein: it lacks essential amino acids, it isn't enough on its own;
- **most modern leather is chrome-tanned**. Chromium, glues, dyes and synthetic soles have no business in a stomach;
- a shoe today often contains more plastic than leather.

**Verdict**: fresh or dried hide, or vegetable-tanned leather (raw, beige, undyed), boiled for a long time, gives a little protein. A sneaker, nothing at all.

## ACT

### Making a real soup from almost nothing

Soup is the best way to feed many people with little: nothing is lost, all the fat and minerals stay in the water, and something hot lifts morale as much as the body.

1. **Fat first.** A piece of bacon, oil, a rind. It's what runs short most in hard times. See [[TEC-ALI-001]].
2. **Something starchy** for calories: potatoes, stale bread, rice, pasta, flour stirred in, oat flakes.
3. **Anything green and edible**: carrot and radish tops, nettles, dandelions, cabbage leaves. See [[SURV-RES-001]].
4. **Bones**, even already gnawed, cracked and simmered for a long time: marrow, fat, calcium.
5. **Salt**, which makes everything edible.

### Making stone soup for real

In a group, a camp, a street after a disaster: **put the pot in the middle, in plain sight**, and announce a soup for everyone. Ask each person for one single thing, a small one. It works better than asking one person for a lot.

## ADAPT

**You really only have leather.** Pick raw hide or undyed leather. Scrape it, cut it into strips, boil it for hours, throw away the first water. Eat the jelly, not the strips.

**The hunger has lasted a long time.** Start eating again very gently, in small amounts, or the body can collapse: this is refeeding syndrome.

**There are children.** They get served first, and they're the ones to send to ask for an onion: nobody says no.

fiches.corps:
::Everyone runs to the hospital pharmacy. It's locked, in the basement, and emptied first. What's valuable is elsewhere, on the wards, and nobody thinks of it.::

## UNDERSTAND

A hospital is a vertical town, organised never to stop. Everything is duplicated and stored close to where it's used: a nurse doesn't go down to the basement for a syringe. That's why **the real stock is spread across the wards**, and the central pharmacy is only part of it.

It's also a place where you find sick people, the dead, and people who need help. If staff are still there, what they know is worth more than anything in the cupboards.

## ACT

### Where to look, in order

**1. The crash carts.** One per ward, red or yellow, in the corridor or near the nurses' station, often closed with a simple plastic seal. Each holds the same thing everywhere: adrenaline, atropine, amiodarone, IV fluids, syringes, cannulas, intubation kit, a bag-valve mask, sometimes a defibrillator on top. **It's full resuscitation, in a kit, laid out in the same order from one hospital to the next.**

**2. The ward stock rooms.** On each ward, a storeroom: dressings, antiseptics, gloves, gauze, drips, common painkillers, frequently used antibiotics. Controlled drugs are in a separate safe; other medicines are freely accessible to staff.

**3. Central sterile services.** Often in the basement or near the operating theatres. Sealed metal boxes, labelled by procedure: forceps, scissors, needle holders, retractors, **already sterile and dated**. A complete suture kit weighs a few hundred grams. See [[TEC-SAN-001]].

**4. The operating theatre.** Suture thread, sterile drapes, head torches, manual suction pumps, gowns.

**5. The maternity ward.** Infant formula, powdered and ready to drink, bottles, teats, nappies, delivery kits. It's what runs out fastest in a city in crisis. See [[URG-SEC-007]].

**6. The kitchen and the laundry.** Food stocks for hundreds of meals, large containers, sheets, blankets, clean gowns.

**7. The plant rooms.** The generator and its fuel tank (hospitals keep several days of autonomy), the UPS batteries, the maintenance team's tools, the pumps.

### Oxygen

Large hospitals have a **liquid oxygen tank** outside, and **cylinders** on the wards and in a storage room. In Europe, a medical oxygen cylinder has a **white shoulder**.

- A 5-litre cylinder full at 200 bar gives about 1,000 litres of oxygen, so **more than 8 hours at 2 litres per minute**.
- Modern cylinders have a built-in regulator with a gauge: you can read what's left.
- **Never grease or oil** on an oxygen valve, never a flame nearby: pure oxygen makes anything greasy burn violently.

## ADAPT

### What not to touch

- **Yellow bins** (sharps and infectious waste): used needles, soiled dressings. They're not supplies.
- **Chemotherapy drugs**, often marked with a purple label or a specific symbol: toxic on contact.
- **Anything with the radiation trefoil**, in nuclear medicine and radiotherapy. In 1987, in Goiânia, Brazil, scrap collectors opened an old caesium source from an abandoned radiotherapy machine. The powder glowed blue in the dark; they showed it to their families. Four people died, hundreds were contaminated. **A very heavy lead container with that symbol is never opened.**
- **Vaccine and insulin fridges** without power for a long time: insulin keeps about a month at room temperature, vaccines much less.

### Expired medicines

The US military had its expired stocks tested for years (the SLEP programme): **the great majority of solid medicines (tablets, capsules) kept their efficacy years after their date**, if stored cool and dry. The exceptions to know: liquids, insulin, adrenaline, eye drops and some antibiotic suspensions lose their efficacy quickly. See [[TEC-SAN-001]].

### Tips you won't find in any manual

- **The outpatient floors** (dermatology, ophthalmology, ENT, dental) are ignored by everyone and full of equipment: lamps, magnifiers, fine instruments, local anaesthetics.
- **Veterinary clinics** have the same antibiotics, antiparasitics and suture thread, in bigger packs, and nobody goes there.
- **The dialysis unit** has a water treatment system: filters, a reverse-osmosis unit, stocks of purified water.
- **The lead aprons** from radiology are heavy but stop X-rays and some low-energy gamma rays.
- **Trolleys, wheelchairs and stretchers** are the best tools to carry what you find. See [[SURV-REC-011]].
- **Bottles of hand sanitiser**, by the pallet, are a disinfectant, a stove fuel and a fire starter.
- **Go in pairs, by day, knowing the way out.** A hospital is a maze of identical corridors, and without power, many fire doors close by themselves. See [[SURV-REC-001]].

fiches.corps:
::A metro train is driven with a single lever. Everything else, the power, the signals, the control room, sits around the train, and that's what makes it run.::

## What moves a train

**Power comes through the track.** On most metros, a **third rail** laid beside the running rails carries direct current, **750 volts** in Paris, 630 in London. A metal shoe under the train slides along it. Other networks use an overhead line, at 1,500 volts.

**Substations** along the lines convert grid power into direct current. **If they go down, everything stops**: a metro train has no engine of its own, only batteries for emergency lighting, doors and the radio.

**The electric motors** are spread under several cars. When braking, they become generators and send current back into the rail: that's electric braking. Friction brakes take over at low speed and to stop.

## The cab

A metro driver has far fewer controls than you'd think:

- **The master controller**, a single lever: pushed, the train accelerates; in neutral, it coasts; pulled, it brakes; all the way, **emergency braking**.
- **The dead man's device**: the driver must keep constant pressure, or release and press again at regular intervals. If not, because they've fainted, the train brakes by itself. In France it's called the **VACMA**.
- **The door controls**, left side and right side, which only open when stopped at a platform.
- **The cab key or badge**, which switches the cab on. A train has a cab at each end; only one is active at a time.
- **The train radio** to the control centre.
- **Screens** showing the permitted speed, faults, door status.

## Signalling: why you can't just floor it

Two trains must never be on the same section. The track is divided into **blocks**, and an occupied block is protected by signals and, above all, by an **automatic train protection system** that brakes the train if it goes over the permitted speed or passes a red signal.

On modern lines, this system is continuous (**CBTC**): the train knows at all times where the one ahead is and adjusts its speed to the metre. That's what allows a train every 85 to 90 seconds at rush hour.

On **driverless lines** (1, 4 and 14 in Paris, Lille, Copenhagen, Dubai, Singapore), there's no driver at all. The central control room runs each train, and platform screen doors close off the platform.

## The control room

A metro is run first of all from a **central control room**: a large room with the layout of the lines, the position of every train, the status of substations, points, tunnel ventilation and pumps. The controllers decide departures, power cuts for maintenance work, the evacuation of a train. The driver carries it out.

## Tips from people who know the tunnels

- **The third rail is always live until proven otherwise.** Even when trains have stopped running. It's often protected by a wooden or plastic cover, but not everywhere. Contact kills. Never step on it, or on its supports.
- **Tunnels have emergency exits** at regular intervals, connected to the surface by stairs and ventilation shafts. They're shown by lit signs and arrows painted on the walls, giving the direction and distance of the nearest station or exit.
- **A train evacuated in a tunnel** is emptied from the front or the back, on orders, once the power is cut. The side doors often open onto the wall or the live rail.
- **Pumps** constantly drain water from the tunnels. Without power for days, the low parts of a network flood, especially near a river.
- **Tunnels have been used as shelters.** In London during the Blitz, up to 177,000 people slept in them on some nights of 1940. They protect from blast and fragments, not from water or stale air once ventilation stops. See [[TEC-CON-009]].
- **A train without power weighs several hundred tonnes.** Without the grid, it doesn't move. Maintenance draisines, small diesel or battery vehicles, and hand trolleys, on the other hand, do run on the rails.

Driving a car and a boat is in [[TEC-VOI-001]] and [[TEC-NAV-001]]. How a station works, and what you find there, is in [[SURV-REC-012]].

fiches.corps:
::A green screen doesn't replace the set. It replaces a colour. All the work is making sure that colour only exists behind you.::

## The principle

The camera films a person in front of a single, even colour. The software finds every pixel of that colour and makes it transparent. Another image slides in behind. That's **keying**, or *chroma key*.

It's the same idea as the TV weather map, film special effects, or the background of any video creator.

## Why green, and why sometimes blue

**Green** is the colour furthest from human skin, whatever its tone. And camera sensors have twice as many green pixels as red or blue: green is the most detailed colour, so the easiest to cut out cleanly.

**Blue** is used when the subject wears green, for night scenes, and gives less coloured reflection on skin. But it needs more light.

Absolute rule: **no clothing, accessory or object in the colour of the screen.** It would become transparent. Watch out for shiny things too, glasses, watches, jewellery: they reflect the screen.

## The three laws of lighting

Lighting makes 80% of the result. Software can't save a badly lit screen.

1. **The screen must be even.** No darker corners, no creases, no glare. Two soft lights at 45 degrees on either side of the screen, rather than one in front.
2. **Light the subject separately**, with their own lights, as for any video.
3. **Keep the subject away from the screen: at least 1.5 to 2 metres** (5 to 6.5 ft). Too close, the green reflects onto shoulders and hair, that's *spill*, and the subject's shadow falls on the screen.

## Camera settings

- **Fast shutter speed** (1/100 s or faster): motion blur mixes subject and green, and the key gets messy.
- **Focus on the subject.** A slightly blurred screen keys even better.
- **Don't overexpose**: a blown-out green becomes almost white.
- **The highest resolution possible**, and a lightly compressed format if the camera offers one.

## The software

Free software is enough: OBS for live, DaVinci Resolve, CapCut or Shotcut for editing. The setting always goes in the same order:

1. pick the colour to remove with the eyedropper, on a mid-tone area of the screen;
2. raise the tolerance until the whole screen disappears, no more;
3. soften the edges a little;
4. turn on **spill suppression**, which removes the green reflection on the outlines.

## Tips from people who do it every day

- **Iron the fabric**, or stretch it on a frame. Every crease makes a shadow, and every shadow is another shade of green. A wall painted matte green beats a creased cloth.
- **Frame wide, crop later.** If the subject goes off the screen, even by a finger, it's lost. Frame the shot, then mask everything outside the screen with a rough mask (*garbage matte*).
- **Fine hair** is the real test. A light placed behind the subject, towards the top of the head, separates hair from the screen and makes the key much cleaner.
- **The final background decides the lighting.** If the new background is a sunset, light the subject warm and from the side. A subject lit like an office, dropped onto a beach, fools no one.
- **No green screen?** A blue sheet, a plain wall, a clear sky behind you. The software accepts any colour, as long as it's even and absent from the subject.
- **New AI tools** cut out subjects without a green screen. They get hands and hair wrong when moving: the green screen stays more reliable as soon as you move.

fiches.corps:
::A wind turbine isn't a bigger windmill. It's a 150-metre power station that turns slowly, runs itself, and needs the grid to exist.::

## The size

A recent onshore wind turbine stands **100 to 200 metres** tall at blade tip, with a rotor **100 to 170 metres** across. Its power: **2 to 6 megawatts**. Offshore, the largest exceed 15 MW, with blades more than 110 metres long.

A blade weighs several tens of tonnes, the nacelle several hundred. The foundation of an onshore turbine is a buried block of reinforced concrete of several hundred cubic metres.

## How it works

**The blades** aren't pushed by the wind like a sail. They have the profile of an aircraft wing: air flowing around them creates lift that makes them turn. See [[TEC-AER-001]].

**The rotor** turns slowly, 5 to 15 revolutions per minute. The blade tips, though, move at more than 250 km/h (155 mph).

**The nacelle**, at the top of the tower, contains:

- **a gearbox** that takes it from 10 to 1,500 revolutions per minute for the generator; or, on "direct-drive" models, a giant permanent-magnet generator with no gearbox;
- **the generator**;
- **the braking system**;
- **power electronics** that match the current to the grid;
- **an anemometer and a wind vane** on the roof.

**Two motors steer it constantly**:

- **yaw** turns the whole nacelle into the wind;
- **pitch** rotates each blade on its own axis to catch more or less wind, as you'd adjust a propeller.

## The power curve

- Below about **3 m/s** (7 mph), it produces nothing.
- Between 3 and about **12 m/s**, power rises very fast: **it varies with the cube of wind speed**. Twice the wind, eight times the energy.
- Above 12 m/s, it levels off at rated power: the blades feather so as not to exceed it.
- Around **25 m/s** (56 mph), it stops and goes into safe mode.

**The Betz limit** says no turbine can capture more than 59.3% of the energy of the wind passing through it: the air has to keep flowing out behind. The best machines reach about 45 to 50%.

Over a year, an onshore turbine produces on average **20 to 30% of its maximum power** (its capacity factor), an offshore one 35 to 50%.

## What's rarely said

**It needs the grid.** Most wind turbines can't start on their own or power an isolated house: their electronics lock onto the frequency of the existing grid, and they use a little power to turn, yaw and heat. **During a blackout, a wind turbine stops**, even in full wind. Only installations specially designed for it can run as an island.

**It's controlled remotely.** Each turbine is monitored from afar by its manufacturer, who can stop it, restart it and read its sensors.

**It lasts 20 to 30 years.** The fibreglass and resin blades recycle badly; the tower, the copper and the steel recycle well.

## Tips from people who work on them

- **Ice gets thrown.** In icy weather, blocks of ice can come off the blades and land tens, even hundreds, of metres away. Signs warn of it at the foot of the machines. Don't stand under an iced-up turbine.
- **You climb on foot.** Many turbines only have an inside ladder with a fall-arrest rail, or a small lift. A hundred metres of ladder: technicians are trained in rescue at height and always work in pairs.
- **Lightning loves wind turbines.** The blades have metal receptors and a cable running down to earth. In a storm, move away.
- **The noise** comes mostly from the blades, a steady whoosh, and the gearbox. At 500 metres, it blends into the wind.
- **A nacelle holds hundreds of litres of oil** (gearbox, hydraulics), plenty of copper and, on direct-drive machines, rare-earth magnets. It's also an observation platform more than 100 metres up. See [[SURV-REC-016]] for what you can take from a big immobile machine.

Small wind turbines, for a house or a boat, work on the same principles but without the grid: see [[TEC-SOLR-001]] for battery storage.

fiches.corps:
::Flutes 40,000 years old have been found, carved from vulture bones. Before writing, before farming, humans were already making music. It isn't a luxury: it's one of the oldest things we do together.::

## Where a sound comes from

A sound is a vibration that moves the air. An instrument always has two parts: **something that vibrates** and **something that amplifies** (a body, a tube, a skin).

The **pitch** of a note depends on the speed of vibration, in vibrations per second (hertz). The tuning A vibrates at 440 Hz. **Doubling the frequency gives the same note, an octave higher.**

For a string, three things raise the note:

- **shortening it** (that's what a finger does on a guitar neck);
- **tightening it**;
- **making it lighter** (a thin string sounds higher than a thick one).

For a tube, its **length** sets the note: the shorter, the higher. The holes of a flute shorten the tube.

## The five families

Museums sort every instrument in the world into five families, according to what vibrates.

| Family | What vibrates | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Idiophones | The instrument itself | Xylophone, balafon, bell, triangle, steel drum, maracas |
| Membranophones | A stretched skin | Drum, djembe, timpani, tabla |
| Chordophones | A string | Guitar, violin, harp, piano, sitar, kora, oud |
| Aerophones | A column of air | Flute, trumpet, saxophone, bagpipes, organ, harmonica, didgeridoo |
| Electrophones | An electric circuit | Synthesizer, electronic organ, theremin |

## Instruments that made history

- **The bone flute**, 40,000 years, Germany: the oldest known instrument.
- **The lyre and the harp**, Mesopotamia, about 4,500 years ago (the lyres of Ur).
- **The drum**, on every continent, for thousands of years.
- **The organ**, born in Greece with the hydraulis in the 3rd century BC, king of Europe's churches in the Middle Ages.
- **The oud**, Middle East, ancestor of the lute and so of the guitar.
- **The sitar**, India, with strings that ring on their own in sympathy.
- **The kora**, West Africa, 21 strings, the instrument of the griots.
- **The violin**, Italy, 16th century; the luthiers of Cremona (Stradivari, Guarneri) fixed it for good.
- **The piano**, Bartolomeo Cristofori, Florence, around 1700: the first keyboard that plays loud or soft depending on the strength of the finger.
- **The accordion and the harmonica**, 19th century: metal reeds, a whole instrument in a pocket.
- **The saxophone**, Adolphe Sax, Belgium, 1846.
- **The steel drum**, Trinidad, 1930s and 1940s: made from abandoned oil drums.
- **The electric guitar**, 1930s to 1950s: a magnetic pickup reads the string, an amplifier does the rest.
- **The synthesizer**, Robert Moog, 1964: sound made entirely by circuits.

## Making one with what you have

The steel drum was born from oil drums, the blues from one-string guitars nailed to a board. **Almost anything can sound.**

- **A whistle**: a hollowed piece of reed or elder, a bevelled notch, a wooden plug leaving a slit. Each hole you drill adds a note.
- **A one-string bass**: an upturned tub, a broom handle resting on its edge, a string stretched from the handle to the centre of the tub. Push the handle to tighten the string and change the note.
- **A box guitar**: a wooden box or a can for the body, a plank for the neck, strings of fishing line, bike brake cable or thin wire.
- **Percussion**: drums, pans, bottles filled with water to different levels (the more water, the higher when tapped).
- **A drum**: a skin or an inner tube stretched over a bucket, tightened with a cord.

## Musicians' tips

- **Tuning without a tuner**: one reference note is enough (a whistle, a bottle; in France, the landline dial tone is an A at 440 Hz). The other strings are tuned to each other by ear, comparing two strings that should play the same note: when the sound "beats" (wobbles), they're off; when it becomes smooth, it's right.
- **Strings wear and sound duller and duller.** Wipe them with a dry cloth after each use; boiling them brings them back a little, an old bass player's trick.
- **Wood moves with humidity.** A wooden instrument is kept away from a stove and a damp wall. A guitar that cracks is almost always a heater that's too close.
- **One instrument per group is enough** to sing together. Music makes time pass, calms children, marks celebrations and mourning. See [[SURV-PSY-001]].

fiches.corps:
::A fallout shelter doesn't protect you from a bomb landing on it. It protects you from what falls from the sky in the two weeks after. Much less spectacular, and much more useful.::

## What you're protecting against

A nuclear explosion acts in four stages, and a shelter doesn't answer each in the same way.

1. **The flash and the heat**, within a second. Any wall stops the flash; it's the fires that follow that kill.
2. **The blast**, a few seconds later. Near ground zero, nothing holds. Further out, it's a wind of several hundred kilometres per hour and a rain of glass.
3. **Initial radiation**, in the first minute, mostly close to the explosion.
4. **Fallout**, for days: dust lifted and made radioactive by a ground burst falls back over tens or hundreds of kilometres downwind. **That's where most lives are saved or lost**, and it's why shelters are built.

## What stops radiation: mass

The gamma rays from fallout go through matter, but each layer stops part of them. This is measured in **halving thickness**: the thickness that cuts radiation in half.

| Material | Halves it | Cuts it 1,000 times (10 layers) |
|---|---|---|
| Steel | 1.8 cm (0.7 in) | 18 cm (7 in) |
| Concrete | 5.6 cm (2.2 in) | 56 cm (22 in) |
| Packed earth | 8.4 cm (3.3 in) | 84 cm (33 in) |
| Water | 12 cm (4.8 in) | 1.2 m (4 ft) |
| Wood | 22 cm (8.8 in) | 2.2 m (7 ft) |

What counts is **the total mass** between you and the dust, above and around. That's why a basement in the middle of a building, under several floors, already protects much better than a single-storey house.

## Time is on your side: the 7-10 rule

Fallout radioactivity drops very fast. **Every time the elapsed time is multiplied by 7, radiation is divided by 10.**

- 7 hours after the explosion: ten times less than after one hour;
- 2 days (49 hours): a hundred times less;
- 2 weeks: a thousand times less.

Hence the advice: **the first 24 to 48 hours matter most.** And hence the stay shelters are designed for: about two weeks.

## How a real shelter is built

Shelters built to standard, as in Switzerland, all share the same elements:

- **a thick reinforced concrete shell**, often underground, which resists the blast at a distance and stops radiation;
- **a sealed blast door** and an airlock, with baffles: radiation travels in straight lines, a bend in a corridor cuts it;
- **filtered ventilation**: a fan, often with a hand crank as backup, draws air through a dust pre-filter then an activated carbon filter, and **keeps the shelter at a slight overpressure**. Dust doesn't get in, even through cracks;
- **blast valves** on air inlets and outlets, which slam shut when the pressure wave arrives;
- **water** for two weeks, dry toilets, bunk beds, battery lighting, a radio;
- **an emergency exit** that doesn't go through the main stairs, often a tunnel or a hatch opening further away, outside the rubble zone.

**Switzerland** is the only country that has guaranteed by law, since 1963, a shelter place for every resident: there are more places than people. Finland, Sweden and Israel also have large networks. France has no shelter network for the public.

## Improvising a shelter

US Army studies showed it: **a well-made expedient shelter protects almost as well** as a built one, against fallout.

- **A basement**: the most underground corner, away from vents. Pile everything heavy against the walls and on the floor above you: sandbags, books, water jugs, full furniture.
- **A covered trench**: a trench a metre wide, as deep as you are tall, covered with doors or planks then 60 to 90 cm (2 to 3 ft) of earth. That's Kearny's shelter, built in 48 hours by ordinary families during trials.
- **A building**: the middle of the building, halfway up or in the basement, away from the roof (where the dust settles) and away from outer walls.

## Tips from people who've studied the question

- **Dust is the real enemy.** When you come in, take off your outer clothes, bag them away from you, wash or wipe yourself, hair included. That removes most of the contamination.
- **Heat kills before radiation** in a packed shelter without ventilation. Kearny designed an expedient fan, the "Kearny air pump", a simple wooden frame with plastic flaps swung by hand.
- **A meter changes everything.** Without a dosimeter, you come out too early or too late. Kearny published plans for an electrometer made with a tin can and aluminium foil.
- **Iodine** only protects the thyroid, and only against radioactive iodine. It isn't an anti-radiation pill. Take it when the authorities say so.
- **Water in the pipes and toilet cisterns**, and in a water heater, is protected from fallout: it can be drunk.
- **Listen to the radio**, battery or hand-cranked. See [[SIG-COM-002]].

Contaminated air and filters are in [[URG-AIR-001]] and [[TEC-SAN-006]].

fiches.corps:
::The sea holds 97% of the planet's water, and you can't drink a glass of it. Desalination means paying in energy for what nature does for free with sun and rain.::

## Why you can't drink seawater

Seawater contains about **35 grams of salt per litre**. Drinking water contains less than 0.5 to 1 gram.

Kidneys can't make urine as salty as the sea. To get rid of the salt in one litre of seawater, they need more than one litre of water. **Drinking seawater dehydrates you faster than drinking nothing.** That's why castaways who drink it die before the others, and what makes desalination essential at sea. See [[TEC-SAN-005]].

## The two big methods

### Heating: distillation

You boil the water, the steam leaves without the salt, you condense it. That's what the sun does above the oceans.

Modern plants don't simply boil: they chain chambers at lower and lower pressure, where water boils at lower and lower temperatures, and recover the heat from each stage to warm the next. These are **multi-stage flash** (MSF) and **multi-effect distillation** (MED). They use a lot of energy, and are found mostly in the Gulf, often paired with power stations whose waste heat they recover.

### Filtering: reverse osmosis

A very thin membrane lets water molecules through and holds back salts. Naturally, water would move towards the saltier side (that's osmosis). **By pushing seawater against the membrane at 55 to 80 bar** (800 to 1,200 psi), you force it through the other way.

This is now the dominant method: **nearly 70% of the world's capacity**. A modern plant uses about **3 to 4 kWh per cubic metre** of fresh water, thanks to recovery devices that reuse the pressure of the outgoing brine.

The process needs:

- **serious pre-treatment**: filtration, sometimes flocculation, so that sand, algae and bacteria don't clog the membranes;
- **post-treatment**: reverse-osmosis water is too pure, aggressive to pipes and poor in minerals. Calcium is added back and the pH corrected.

## The numbers

- The world desalinates **about 95 million cubic metres a day** (late 2010s), in more than 15,000 plants.
- The Middle East and North Africa produce nearly half. Saudi Arabia, the Emirates and Israel depend on it for a large share of their drinking water.
- The largest reverse-osmosis plant in the world, at Sorek in Israel, produces more than 600,000 m³ a day.
- From 100 litres of seawater, a reverse-osmosis plant returns **about 40 to 50 of fresh water**. The rest goes back as **brine**, twice as salty as the sea.

## What doesn't work so well

**Energy.** Even efficient, a plant uses ten times more than pumping fresh water. A power cut stops it, and tap water with it.

**Brine.** Released into the sea, it sinks to the bottom and can smother local life if it isn't well diffused. It also carries pre-treatment chemicals.

**Membranes** foul and are replaced every five to ten years. They are made by a handful of manufacturers.

**The target.** A desalination plant is a single piece of infrastructure feeding an entire city. The Gulf countries protect them like power stations.

## At small scale

- **The manual watermaker** in life rafts: a small hand-pumped reverse-osmosis unit that makes a few litres an hour. It's the one piece of equipment that really changes survival at sea.
- **Boat watermakers**: electric, from 20 to several hundred litres an hour. They live on the boat's batteries and solar panels.
- **The solar still**: a black tank under a sloping pane of glass. It makes around **2 to 5 litres per square metre per day** in full sun. Slow, but with no moving parts.
- **Old sea ice is almost fresh**: as it freezes, water pushes the salt out. Bluish, rounded ice more than a year old can be drunk once melted. Young, grey, opaque ice stays salty.

## Tips you learn at sea

- **Never keep the first water** from a watermaker after it has been stopped: it's salty. Taste it before filling the tank.
- **A membrane that dries out dies.** When stopped, it's kept wet with a storage solution, or run regularly.
- **Near a port or a river mouth**, seawater is polluted with hydrocarbons and discharges: they damage membranes and aren't all held back. Desalinate offshore.
- **Rain is still the best fresh water at sea.** A tarp stretched into a funnel gives more than a still. See [[SURV-PLUIE-001]].

fiches.corps:
::An explosive isn't something that burns hard. It's a reaction that travels faster than sound through the material itself. The whole difference between a quarry and an accident lies in that sentence.::

## Burning, deflagrating, detonating

**Combustion** needs oxygen from the air. It advances as fast as the air arrives: a wood fire.

**A deflagration** carries its own oxygen. The reaction spreads from grain to grain through heat, at a few metres to a few hundred metres per second. Confined, it builds pressure until the container bursts. That's black powder, and the powder in a cartridge.

**A detonation** travels as a shock wave through the material, at 2,000 to 9,000 metres per second. It doesn't need confinement: it shatters what it touches. That's dynamite, TNT, military explosives.

## The families

**Primary explosives** detonate at the slightest shock, friction, spark or heat. They're used in tiny amounts, in detonators, to start the chain. They're also the most dangerous to handle, and the ones that most often kill amateur makers.

**Secondary explosives** are stable: you can often burn them without them detonating. They need the shock of a detonator. Almost everything used in practice belongs to this family.

Hence the **explosive train**, the same everywhere: a detonator (primary, a few tenths of a gram), sometimes a booster, then the main charge (secondary). Each stage wakes the next. Without a detonator, a block of military explosive is an inert material you can set down, cut, or even burn, which doesn't mean you should.

## The explosives that mattered

| Name | Era | Family | What to know |
|---|---|---|---|
| Black powder | China, 9th century | Deflagrating | Charcoal, sulphur, saltpetre. Made cannons and mines for 800 years. |
| Nitroglycerin | 1847 | Secondary, very sensitive | A liquid unstable to shock. Unusable as is. |
| Dynamite | Nobel, 1867 | Secondary | Nitroglycerin soaked into a porous earth. Made tunnels and railways possible. |
| TNT | 1863, military from 1902 | Secondary, very stable | Melts without detonating, is poured into shells. Used as a unit of measure. |
| ANFO | 1950s | Secondary | Ammonium nitrate and fuel oil. The most used civil explosive in the world, in mines and quarries. |
| Emulsions | 1960s | Secondary | Nitrate-based pastes, water-resistant. They replaced dynamite. |
| RDX, PETN | Second World War | Secondary, powerful | The bases of military plastic explosives (C-4, Semtex) and detonating cord. |

**Ammonium nitrate** deserves a line of its own: it's first of all a fertiliser, stored by the thousand tonnes. Badly stored, it caused the disasters of Toulouse (AZF plant, 2001, 31 dead) and Beirut (port, 2020, more than 200 dead).

## What they're used for

- **Mines and quarries**: by far the first use. Every day, thousands of tonnes of explosive break rock.
- **Tunnels and mountain roads.**
- **Demolition** of buildings and structures: the load-bearing columns are cut in the right order, and the building falls in on itself.
- **Preventive avalanche release**, at ski resorts.
- **Seismic surveys**: small charges send waves into the ground to look for oil or study what lies beneath.
- **Airbags, ejection seats, explosive bolts** on rockets: tiny charges that act in milliseconds.
- **War**, of course.

The people who use them, **shotfirers** or blasters, are trained and licensed. In France as almost everywhere, making, holding or transporting an explosive without authorisation is a serious offence.

## The effects

An explosion injures in three ways:

- **The pressure wave**, which tears lungs, eardrums and intestines. It weakens very quickly with distance.
- **Fragments**, which carry much further than the wave. They're what sets safety distances.
- **Heat and falls**: burns, being thrown, collapses.

The US National Counterterrorism Center publishes indicative evacuation distances, which give the order of magnitude:

| Device | Amount | Evacuate buildings within | Outdoors, move away to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pipe bomb | 2 kg (5 lb) | 21 m (70 ft) | 366 m (1,200 ft) |
| Bag, suitcase | 23 kg (50 lb) | 46 m (150 ft) | 564 m (1,850 ft) |
| Car | 230 kg (500 lb) | 98 m (320 ft) | 457 m (1,500 ft) |
| Van | 450 kg (1,000 lb) | 122 m (400 ft) | 732 m (2,400 ft) |

**What people who've seen it remember:** it isn't the metres that protect you, it's what stands between you and the charge. A thick wall, an earth bank, the corner of a building. And **windows**: most of the injured in an urban explosion are hurt by glass, sometimes hundreds of metres away. Stay away from windows.

## Field tips

- **Old explosive is more dangerous than new.** Old dynamite "sweats": nitroglycerin seeps out and forms crystals or oily drops on the sticks or the cardboard. At that stage, a knock is enough. Don't touch it again, call bomb disposal.
- **"Turn off radio transmitters" signs** near blasting sites are no joke. Some electric detonators can be set off by a powerful transmitter close by. Walkie-talkies and phones off near a blast.
- **A smell of almonds or solvent, or a headache** near an old stock: some nitrate-based explosives are absorbed through the skin and cause violent migraines, the "dynamite headache" well known to miners.
- **A wire sticking out, a new box in an abandoned place, an object that has no reason to be there**: you don't know, so you don't touch. Mark the spot and leave the way you came.
- **Wartime leftovers** still kill farmers and walkers every year, in France and elsewhere. See [[SURV-REC-010]].

## If you find some

1. Don't touch, don't move, don't cut anything.
2. Walk away the way you came, and keep others away.
3. Mark the spot from a distance, with something visible.
4. Call the police or the fire service (112 in Europe). Bomb disposal comes out for free.
5. No radio or phone next to the object: call once, from a distance.

Firearm ballistics are in [[TEC-BAL-001]] and [[TEC-BAL-002]].

fiches.corps:
::A cartridge is four parts and a name. The name tells you almost everything, if you know how to read it, and it's what prevents the accident.::

## What's in a cartridge

**The case**, usually brass, sometimes lacquered steel or aluminium. It holds everything together, and when fired it expands against the chamber to seal it.

**The primer**, in the base. A small shock-sensitive charge, struck by the firing pin, that sends a flame into the powder.

**The powder**, today smokeless, based on nitrocellulose. It doesn't detonate: it burns very fast and makes gas that pushes.

**The projectile**, the bullet. Bare lead, copper-jacketed lead, solid copper, sometimes with a steel core.

Two big families of priming:

- **Rimfire**: the priming compound sits in the rim of the base. The firing pin crushes the edge. That's the .22 LR. These cartridges can't be reloaded.
- **Centerfire**: a round primer in the centre of the base. Almost all the others. The case can be reloaded.

## Reading a caliber name

**The metric system** gives two numbers: bullet diameter, then case length, in millimetres. 9 × 19 mm, 7.62 × 39 mm, 5.56 × 45 mm.

**The imperial system** gives the diameter in hundredths or thousandths of an inch, followed by a name: .22 Long Rifle, .45 ACP, .308 Winchester.

**The same round often has several names.** 9 × 19 mm is also called 9 mm Parabellum, 9 mm Luger or 9 mm NATO. The .380 ACP is the 9 × 17 mm, also called 9 mm Short or 9 mm Kurz.

**And two different rounds sometimes share a number.** The 9 mm Makarov (9 × 18 mm) is not a 9 × 19. The 7.62 × 39 (Kalashnikov) has nothing to do with the 7.62 × 51 (NATO) or the 7.62 × 54R (Mosin-Nagant, Dragunov). **Always read the full marking, never just the number.**

The marking is stamped on the case base (the headstamp): maker, caliber, sometimes year. On the gun, the caliber is engraved on the barrel or the slide. **The two must match exactly.**

## Common calibers

Typical values, which vary with the load and the barrel length.

| Caliber | Other names | Use | Bullet | Velocity | Energy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| .22 LR | 22 long rifle, 5.6 mm | Target, small game | 2.6 g (40 gr) | 330 m/s | 140 J |
| .380 ACP | 9 × 17, 9 mm Short | Pocket pistol | 6.2 g | 290 m/s | 260 J |
| 9 × 18 Makarov | 9 mm PM | Former Eastern-bloc pistols | 6.1 g | 315 m/s | 300 J |
| 9 × 19 | 9 mm Parabellum, Luger, NATO | Pistol and submachine gun, the most common in the world | 8 g (124 gr) | 360 m/s | 500 J |
| .38 Special | 38 Spl | Revolver | 10.2 g | 270 m/s | 370 J |
| .357 Magnum | 357 Mag | Revolver, also fires .38 Special | 10.2 g | 400 m/s | 800 J |
| .40 S&W | 10 × 22 | Police pistol (United States) | 11.7 g | 330 m/s | 640 J |
| .45 ACP | 11.43 × 23 | Pistol | 15 g (230 gr) | 255 m/s | 490 J |
| 5.56 × 45 NATO | .223 Remington (close) | Western assault rifle | 4 g | 940 m/s | 1,750 J |
| 7.62 × 39 | 7.62 Soviet, M43 | Kalashnikov, SKS | 8 g | 715 m/s | 2,050 J |
| 7.62 × 51 NATO | .308 Winchester (close) | Precision rifle, machine gun, hunting | 9.5 g | 850 m/s | 3,400 J |
| 7.62 × 54R | 7.62 Russian | Mosin-Nagant, Dragunov, PKM | 9.6 g | 830 m/s | 3,300 J |
| .30-06 Springfield | 7.62 × 63 | Hunting, older rifles | 11.7 g | 820 m/s | 3,900 J |
| 12.7 × 99 NATO | .50 BMG | Heavy machine gun, anti-materiel | 42 g | 900 m/s | 17,000 J |
| 12 gauge slug | | Shotgun, big game | 28 g | 450 m/s | 2,800 J |

To compare these energies and understand what they do to a target, see [[TEC-BAL-001]].

## The shotgun: caliber backwards

For smoothbore guns, the "gauge" is a number of lead balls: a 12 gauge barrel has the diameter of a lead ball weighing one twelfth of a pound. **The bigger the number, the smaller the barrel.** A 12 gauge is about 18.5 mm, a 20 gauge about 15.6 mm. The .410 is the exception: it's a true diameter in inches.

Three main loads:

- **Birdshot** (sizes 6 to 9): birds, small game. It loses its energy within a few dozen metres.
- **Buckshot**: about ten large pellets. Big game at short range, defence.
- **Slug**: a single heavy projectile, for big game.

Shell length matters too: 65, 70 or 76 mm (2½, 2¾ or 3 in). A shell too long for the chamber raises pressure dangerously.

## Bullet types

- **Full metal jacket (FMJ)**: lead core fully covered in copper. It goes through and deforms little. Standard military round.
- **Jacketed hollow point (JHP)**: a cavity at the front. It opens on impact, transfers its energy, goes through less. Police and defence round.
- **Soft point (SP)**: exposed lead at the front that flattens in a controlled way. The classic hunting round.
- **Tracer**: a compound in the base burns in flight and shows the trajectory. It can start a fire in dry grass.
- **Armour-piercing**: hard steel or tungsten core, to go through protection.
- **Subsonic**: under 340 m/s, so no supersonic crack. Useful with a suppressor.

## What can't be swapped

**A cartridge is only fired in the gun made for it.** The exceptions are known and limited:

- a .357 Magnum revolver fires .38 Special, not the reverse;
- a gun chambered in 5.56 NATO fires .223 Remington; the reverse is not advised, 5.56 runs at higher pressure;
- a gun in 7.62 × 51 generally fires .308 Winchester.

Everything else is a bet on the strength of the gun and your hands. **A 9 × 18 in a 9 × 19 gun can fire badly; a 7.62 × 39 won't fit a 7.62 × 51 and the other way round.**

## Tips from people who've handled it

- **The base doesn't lie.** A primer struck but not fired (a hang fire): keep the gun pointed in a safe direction for at least 30 seconds before opening. The round can still go off.
- **A green primer or a case pitted with verdigris**: don't fire it, it has taken on moisture.
- **Eastern-bloc military ammunition** often has corrosive primers (potassium chlorate): after shooting, clean the barrel with hot water, or it rusts within days.
- **Storage**: cool, dry, away from temperature swings. A military metal ammo can with a seal, and a desiccant sachet. Well stored, modern ammunition lasts decades. See [[SURV-MUN-001]].
- **Weight**: a thousand rounds of 9 mm weigh about 12 kg (26 lb); of .22 LR, about 3.5 kg (8 lb). That's why the .22 LR remains the most practical trade good of its kind.
- **A cartridge thrown in a fire** isn't a fired bullet: without a barrel, the case bursts and throws fragments, but the bullet leaves at low speed. Dangerous for the eyes, rarely more.

## The law

In France, ammunition follows the category of the gun: buying it generally requires the same permit as the gun (shooting licence, hunting licence, authorisation). Rules vary widely from country to country. A gun or ammunition you find is reported to the police: see [[SURV-ARM-001]].

fiches.corps:
::Two different metals and a little vinegar make electricity. Not enough to charge a phone, but enough to light a lamp in the dark, and with nothing, that's already a lot.::

## UNDERSTAND

A battery is **two different metals** that don't touch, with **an electrolyte** between them: a liquid or paste that carries charge, salt water, vinegar, lemon juice. The metal most "eager" to dissolve (zinc, aluminium, magnesium) gives up electrons, which travel through the wire to the other side. See [[TEC-ENE-012]].

**The voltage depends on the pair of metals**, not on size:

| Pair | Voltage per cell, roughly |
|---|---|
| Zinc and copper | 0.8 to 1 V |
| Aluminium and charcoal (aluminium-air cell) | 0.7 to 1.2 V |
| Magnesium and copper | 1.5 to 2 V |
| Iron and copper | 0.3 to 0.5 V |

**The current depends on the surface area** of the metals and the quality of the electrolyte. The bigger, the more it delivers.

**For more voltage**, you put several cells in series: the copper of one joined to the zinc of the next. That's exactly what Volta did in 1800 with his "pile" of stacked discs, which gave its name to all the batteries after it.

**The reality, to know before you start:** a lemon gives about 0.9 volts and **less than a milliamp**. A phone needs 5 volts and about one amp to charge. You'd need thousands of lemons. A makeshift battery is for **an LED, a calculator, a clock, a small signal**, not for charging a device.

## ACT

### The coin battery (the most practical)

You need: copper or copper-coloured coins (1, 2 and 5 euro cent coins are copper-plated steel and work; so do old copper pennies), **galvanised** washers (grey, zinc-coated, from the hardware aisle), cardboard, salt or vinegar.

1. Cut rounds of cardboard or kitchen paper slightly smaller than the coins.
2. Soak them in very salty water or vinegar, then let them drip: **damp, not dripping**, otherwise the liquid bridges the cells and everything stops.
3. Stack: coin, cardboard, washer, coin, cardboard, washer… Each trio gives about 0.5 to 0.8 V.
4. Six to eight layers are enough for a red LED; ten to twelve for a white one.
5. The bottom wire touches the first coin (plus), the top wire the last washer (minus). The LED goes **the right way round**: long leg towards the copper. See [[TEC-ELN-004]].
6. Hold the stack together with a rubber band or inside a piece of tube.

### The aluminium-air cell (the one that delivers most)

1. A sheet of **kitchen foil** laid flat.
2. On top, kitchen paper soaked in **saturated salt water**.
3. On top, a layer of **charcoal crushed to powder**, moistened with the same salt water (activated carbon from a filter works best).
4. Press a copper wire, a pencil lead or a metal plate onto the charcoal, without touching the foil: that's plus. The foil is minus.

A single hand-sized cell can give about one volt and a few tens of milliamps. Two or three in series light an LED for several hours, until the aluminium is eaten away.

### The fruit or vegetable battery

A galvanised nail and a coin or copper wire pushed into a lemon, a potato or a jar of sauerkraut, two or three centimetres apart. Three or four in series make a red LED glow faintly. Boiling the potato first makes a clear difference.

## ADAPT

**You have no multimeter.** Test each cell on your tongue, the way old electricians tested a 9 V battery: a slight tingle means there's voltage. Only on these small homemade cells, never on anything else. Better: see [[TEC-ENE-008]].

**The LED won't light.** Turn it round. Then check that no liquid runs from one cell to the next. Then add cells.

**You really want energy.** Homemade cells aren't the answer. Salvage battery cells from a laptop ([[SURV-REC-021]]), a scooter or a cordless tool, and recharge them from the sun or a dynamo: see [[SURV-ENE-001]].

**You want to listen to the radio.** A crystal set needs no battery at all: the energy comes from the radio wave itself. See [[TEC-RAD-001]].

**Homemade cells run down** when the zinc or aluminium is eaten away: replace the washer or the foil, and re-soak the cardboard. They can be rebuilt forever, as long as there's metal.

fiches.corps:
::A Phenix device should be buildable from parts found everywhere, repairable with a soldering iron, and hold the whole library in a pocket. Everything is open: the plans, the code, the mistakes.::

**Everything below is at prototype stage.** Nothing is for sale. The 3D renders of the devices are concepts; only the WiFi hotspot has already worked on a real phone.

## The two devices

**Phenix 001, the small one.** A pocket reader, no bigger than a small remote control, holding the whole library on a memory card and showing it on a small, frugal screen. Common parts, a case you open with a screwdriver, a replaceable battery.

**Phenix 002, the big one.** A larger device, with a colour screen wide enough to read maps. Two memory card slots under a rubber flap: it can **read a Phenix 001's card, check its library and repair damaged sheets**. Modules plug onto pins: solar panel, dynamo, lamp. And a broken Phenix should be able to run again on a salvaged screen, even one from an old payment terminal.

## What already exists: the Phenix hotspot

This is the first prototype that works. An electronic board costing a few euros opens a WiFi network called **Phenix**, with no password. **Any phone that connects to it opens the whole library**, without internet and without installing anything: the page opens by itself, like a hotel WiFi portal.

**The parts**

| Part | Role | Rough price |
|---|---|---|
| ESP32-C3 "Super Mini" | The brain and the WiFi | 3 to 5 € |
| USB-C cable | Power and programming | already at home |
| Power bank | Battery life | already at home |
| Micro SD card module (optional) | For a bigger library | 1 to 2 € |

**Two versions**

- **Without an SD card**: the full app, compressed (under one megabyte), is written straight into the board's memory. Nothing to solder. This is the version that worked.
- **With an SD card**: the library sits on a FAT32 micro SD card, prepared on the computer. Wiring: CS to GPIO7, MOSI to GPIO6, SCK to GPIO4, MISO to GPIO5, plus 3.3 V and ground.

**Building it**

1. Install **Arduino IDE 2**, add Espressif's ESP32 boards, choose the **ESP32C3 Dev Module** board.
2. In the Tools menu: **Partition Scheme: Huge APP**, and **USB CDC On Boot: Enabled**.
3. Open the hotspot program, in the **materiel/phenix-001-v0** folder of the repository, and upload.
4. If the upload won't start: unplug, **hold the BOOT button down**, plug back in, release, try again.
5. On the phone: WiFi settings, network **Phenix**. If the page doesn't open by itself, type **192.168.4.1** in the browser.

## What was tried, and what we learned

**The screen of an old Nokia phone**: the idea was to reuse the colour screen of a dead phone. Two obstacles stopped it: a 24-pin connector with pins 0.4 mm apart, almost impossible to solder without fine equipment, and a backlight needing about 13 volts. **Lesson**: for a device everyone must be able to rebuild, a screen module sold for microcontrollers, already on its small board, beats an exotic salvaged part. See [[TEC-ELN-001]].

**Next planned**: a 2.8-inch colour screen with a built-in SD card reader, or a 2.9-inch **electronic ink** screen, which keeps its page without power and reads in full sun, see [[TEC-ELN-003]].

## The principles behind the design

- **Parts found everywhere**, online and in electronics shops, replaceable one by one.
- **Everything is documented**: schematics, code, parts list, in the public repository. A device whose insides nobody knows can't be repaired.
- **The library stays readable without the device**: they're the same text files as everywhere else. An SD card pulled from a broken Phenix reads on any computer.
- **Energy first**: a device that must last far from sockets picks its components for their consumption before their power.

The project as a whole is presented in [[TEC-IDE-008]].
