fiches.corps:
::Phenix is a library of practical knowledge that works without the internet, that anyone can read, correct and grow. It doesn't bet on the end of the world. It bets that knowledge should be there on the day you need it.::

## What it is

Phenix gathers **sheets**: how to find water, fix a tyre, treat a burn, read a circuit breaker, make soup for twenty out of almost nothing. Each sheet is a simple **text file**. The software sorts them, links them and filters them, but **if Phenix disappears, the sheets stay readable** in any text editor. That principle governs everything else. The format of a sheet is described in [[TEC-IDE-003]].

## The three axes

- **Axis 1, Memory**: what happened, and what it teaches us.
- **Axis 2, Technique**: how something works, with the numbers, plans and tables that go with it.
- **Axis 3, Survival**: what to do, now, when things go wrong.

When a subject belongs to two axes, we write both sheets and link them. We never write the same thing twice.

## The three building blocks

- **Phenix Base**, the app: on a phone, a computer, or simply in a browser. It works entirely offline: sheets, search, saved maps, markers, reading lists, inventory, notes. Your data stays with you.
- **Phenix Lab**, when there's a connection: suggest an idea or a whole sheet, vote for what's useful, comment, share a map or a layer of markers.
- **Phenix Hub**: every version of the library. The official one, and those that communities publish for their language, region or group. You choose the one you read, build your own by ticking axes, categories, sheets, maps and layers, and share it.

## What sets it apart

- **Open**: anyone can write a sheet, on any useful subject. The limits come after, not before.
- **Participative**: people suggest, vote, correct and discuss. On specialist subjects, those who know debate until they reach a consensus.
- **Practical**: knowledge that says how to **do** and how to **fix**, not just how something works.
- **No account, no required server, no advertising.** The connection is only used for sharing features.

## Licences

- **The sheets** are under the **Creative Commons BY-SA 4.0** licence: you can copy, print, translate, modify and redistribute them, even to sell a book, as long as you credit Phenix and keep your changes under the same licence.
- **The app's code** is under the **MIT** licence.

## Contributing, in practice

1. **Write a sheet**: the "+ Sheet" button in the app, then "Suggest to the corpus". Without a connection, export it as .md and drop it on Phenix Lab later.
2. **Vote and comment** on other people's suggestions on Phenix Lab: that's what brings the best ones up.
3. **Translate**: a translated sheet keeps the same identifier and becomes readable in another language.
4. **Map**: a layer of markers (springs, shelters, crossing points) for your area, shared on Phenix Hub.
5. **Build a device**: the plans and code of the prototypes are open, see [[TEC-IDE-009]].

## What isn't there yet

The project is young and says so. The corpus holds a few hundred sheets where it aims for thousands. The online features are recent. Sheets aren't digitally signed yet. The devices are prototypes. All of this moves forward one sheet at a time, and faster when there are many of us.

## Where to find it

- The website, the online app and downloads: **anthrophobicc.github.io/PhenixProject**
- The code and the sheets: the **PhenixProject** repository on GitHub
- New sheets, week after week: **@phenixprjct** on Instagram

Knowledge doesn't go out as long as someone keeps it.

fiches.corps:
::A battery is a chemical reaction put on pause in a can. Closing the circuit restarts it, and it stops when one of its two ingredients runs out.::

## Single-use or rechargeable

**A primary cell**, what most people call a battery, empties once. **A rechargeable battery** (an accumulator) recharges hundreds of times. Rechargeables have their own sheet: [[TEC-ENE-004]].

Inside a cell, two different materials with an electrolyte between them. One gives up electrons, the other takes them: the electrons go round through the outside circuit, and that current is what we use. The principle is so simple you can make one with two metals and vinegar, see [[SURV-ENE-002]].

## The families

| Type | Voltage | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zinc-carbon ("heavy duty") | 1.5 V | Very cheap | Low capacity, leaks easily |
| Alkaline | 1.5 V | The standard, good capacity at low drain | Loses a lot under heavy drain and in the cold, can leak |
| 1.5 V lithium (AA, AAA sizes) | 1.5 V | Light, works down to −40 °C, keeps 20 years | More expensive |
| 3 V lithium (CR2032, CR123A) | 3 V | Long life; watches, car keys, tactical torches | Different voltage: doesn't replace two 1.5 V cells just anywhere |
| Silver oxide (button cells) | 1.55 V | Very steady voltage, watches | Small capacity |
| Zinc-air (hearing aids) | 1.4 V | Huge capacity for its size | Activated by pulling off the sticker, spent within weeks after that |

## Sizes

| Common name | IEC designation | Size |
|---|---|---|
| AAA | LR03 | 10.5 × 44.5 mm |
| AA | LR6 | 14.5 × 50.5 mm |
| C | LR14 | 26.2 × 50 mm |
| D | LR20 | 34.2 × 61.5 mm |
| 9 V | 6LR61 | six small cells in series in one case |

**Capacity isn't fixed.** An alkaline AA gives about 2,500 to 3,000 mAh in a clock or a remote, but less than half that in a hungry device like a camera flash or a motorised toy. For those uses, lithium cells or rechargeables do far better.

## Storing batteries

- **How long**: 5 to 10 years for alkaline, 10 to 20 years for lithium, in good conditions. The expiry date is printed on the cell.
- **Where**: cool, dry, at a steady temperature. The fridge adds almost nothing for modern alkalines, and condensation when you take them out can harm them.
- **How**: in their packaging or a box, terminals protected. A loose 9 V battery in a drawer can touch a metal object, heat up and start a fire.
- **Not in stored devices**: an alkaline forgotten in a torch will eventually leak and eat the contacts.

## Tips from people who use a lot of them

- **The white crust** on a leaking alkaline is potassium hydroxide, a corrosive base. Clean it with a cotton bud dipped in **vinegar or lemon juice** (the acid neutralises the base), then rub the contacts with an eraser or a fine file. Gloves and glasses if there's a lot.
- **The bounce test**: dropped upright onto a hard table from about ten centimetres, a fresh alkaline lands with a dull thud, a spent one bounces. It's approximate, but real: as it discharges, the inside of the cell changes consistency.
- **Never mix** new and used cells, or two brands or types in the same device: the weakest gets "reversed" by the others and leaks.
- **Recharging an ordinary alkaline** is not advised: it heats, leaks or swells. To recharge, use low self-discharge NiMH cells (1.2 V): they keep most of their charge for years and replace alkalines almost everywhere.
- **Cold drains an alkaline**: keep spare batteries in an inside pocket, and warm a cold one against your body before deciding it's dead.
- **A button battery swallowed by a child is an absolute emergency.** Within a few hours it burns the oesophagus. Go straight to the emergency room, don't make the child vomit. Keep them out of reach, and the same goes for remotes whose battery cover opens easily.

Used batteries go back to the shop for recycling: they contain metals that can be recovered.

fiches.corps:
::A circuit breaker doesn't protect your appliances. It protects your wires from fire, and the RCD protects your body. When it trips, it's telling you something: understand what before you switch it back on.::

## What it watches

An electric wire heats up when current flows through it. Too much current and it gets hot enough to melt its insulation and start a fire inside the wall. **The breaker cuts first.** It watches for two different dangers, with two mechanisms:

- **Overload**: too many appliances on the same circuit. The current is a little too high, for a long time. A **bimetallic strip** (two metals bonded together that expand differently) heats, bends and trips the breaker after a few seconds to a few minutes.
- **Short circuit**: two wires touching. The current becomes enormous at once. A **coil** creates a magnetic field that opens the contact within a few milliseconds.

## Reading a breaker

**The rating**, in amps, is printed on it: the current it lets through continuously. In France, the standard ties the rating to the size of the wire it protects (other countries have their own tables, on the same principle):

| Circuit | Wire | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Lighting | 1.5 mm² | 10 A (16 A allowed) |
| Ordinary sockets | 1.5 mm² or 2.5 mm² | 16 A or 20 A |
| Washing machine, dishwasher, oven | 2.5 mm² | 20 A |
| Hob | 6 mm² | 32 A |

**Never a higher rating than the wire can take.** Replacing a 16 A breaker that keeps tripping with a 32 A one removes the protection: the wire will heat until something burns.

**The letter** in front of the rating (B, C or D) says when it cuts instantly: C for ordinary household use, B for long runs, D for motors with a hard start.

## The RCD: the one that saves lives

Current that leaves by the live wire must come back by the neutral. If some is missing, it's escaping somewhere else: through a wet appliance, a damaged wire, **or a person**. The **residual current device** (RCD) compares the two and cuts as soon as the difference reaches its threshold: **30 milliamps** for those protecting people, within a few tens of milliseconds. Fast enough that an electric shock doesn't become electrocution.

- It has a **test button**: press it once a month, it must cut cleanly.
- It comes as **type AC** and **type A**: in France, type A is required on hob and washing machine circuits, whose electronics produce leaks a type AC can miss.

**The main switch** near the meter cuts the whole house. It is often residual-current too, with a higher threshold and a slight delay, so that the 30 mA devices act first.

## It tripped: read the message

- **It trips again immediately** when switched back on: a **short circuit**. Unplug everything on that circuit, switch on, then plug in one appliance at a time. The culprit trips it when plugged back in.
- **It trips after a few minutes**, when everything runs at once: an **overload**. Spread appliances across other circuits.
- **The RCD trips**: a **leak**. Look for water: an outdoor socket, a bathroom, an appliance that took on moisture, a water heater. Same method: unplug everything, switch on, plug back in one at a time.
- **It trips during storms**: a surge, or water getting in somewhere.

## An electrician's tips

- **Never hold the lever up** to stop a breaker tripping. Modern ones cut anyway, old ones don't, and that's how fires start.
- **A breaker that's warm or smells hot** almost always has a loose terminal screw. A bad contact heats up, see [[TEC-ENE-003]].
- **Label your panel** on a day when everything works. On the day you need to cut the kitchen in the dark, you won't have time to search.
- **Old fuses** are replaced with a fuse of the same rating, never with copper wire or kitchen foil.
- **Before power returns after a long outage**, switch off circuits for fragile or dangerous appliances (heaters, oven, pumps), and switch them back on one by one: the grid often comes back with surges.
- **A generator is never connected to a wall socket** with a cable with two male plugs. It would feed power back into the grid and can kill a technician working on the line hundreds of metres away. It needs a transfer switch, fitted by an electrician. See [[URG-RES-001]].

sources: French Lighting Association (AFE), Recommendations for public road lighting
Regulation (EC) No 245/2009 on ecodesign of discharge lamps (end of mercury vapour lamps in 2015)
CEREMA, Public lighting: a guide for local authorities
French decree of 27 December 2018 on the prevention and limitation of light pollution
fiches.corps:
::A street light decides nothing. A sensor tells it night has fallen, a cabinet on the corner sends it power, and someone at the town hall chose the hour it switches off.::

## How a street lights up

**The control cabinet.** Street lights aren't wired to the grid one by one. They form circuits of a few dozen lights, fed by a grey metal **cabinet**, often at the foot of a wall or next to a transformer. It holds the protection, the meter and the switching.

**Switching** turns the whole circuit on and off at once:

- either by a **photocell**, a small light sensor on the cabinet or on a lamp post, which switches on when daylight drops below a threshold;
- or by an **astronomical clock**, which works out sunset and sunrise for the town every day;
- more and more, by **remote management**: each light gets its orders remotely and can dim in the middle of the night.

**Night switch-off.** Thousands of French towns turn off part of their lighting in the dead of night, often between midnight and 5 am, to save energy and limit light pollution. The law also governs the direction and colour of the light.

## The pole

A lamp post stands **4 to 12 metres** (13 to 40 ft) tall depending on the road: low in pedestrian streets, tall on highways. The column is a hollow tube of galvanised steel or aluminium. **At the base, a small hatch** gives access to the connection box and the fuse for that light.

## Lamps, from oldest to newest

| Lamp | Light | What to know |
|---|---|---|
| Gas | Soft yellow | City lighting in the 19th century. A lamplighter came by every evening with his pole. |
| Mercury vapour | Bluish white | Banned from sale in the European Union since 2015, still in place in forgotten corners. |
| Low-pressure sodium | Pure orange | Very efficient, but a single colour: under it, you can't tell red from green. |
| High-pressure sodium | Golden orange | The light of roads and cities for forty years. Takes several minutes to reach full brightness. |
| Metal halide | White | Squares, stadiums, monuments. |
| LED | White, warmer or cooler | The standard today. Half the energy of sodium, instant on, dimmable. |

## The solar street light

In car parks, on cycle paths and at isolated stops, more and more street lights are **self-contained**: a solar panel at the top of the pole, a battery (often lithium iron phosphate) in the pole or under the panel, a charge controller, an LED head and a motion sensor. No cable connects them to the grid. See [[TEC-SOLR-001]].

## What the maintenance crews know

- **Orange light hides colours.** Under sodium lighting, a map, colour-coded wiring or a wound is hard to read. A white head torch changes everything.
- **During a general blackout, solar street lights stay on.** They're often the only light in a neighbourhood. And each is a complete, self-contained kit: panel, battery, controller, LED light, which once taken down can light a room or charge a small battery. See [[SURV-ENE-001]].
- **The hatch at the base of the pole is live.** The supply cable is connected there at 230 volts, sometimes more. A hatch torn off after a crash gets reported, not explored.
- **Cover a photocell** and it thinks it's night: that's how technicians test lights in broad daylight. A photocell covered in bird droppings or badly aimed explains a street lit at noon.
- **A street light that blinks** at the end of its life is almost always a sodium lamp that switches off as it heats up and comes back on as it cools.
- **Lighting attracts insects**, especially under white and blue light. That's one reason for moving to warmer, orange-tinted LEDs near natural areas.

sources: Schubert E. F., Light-Emitting Diodes, Cambridge University Press, 2nd edition
Nobel Foundation, Nobel Prize in Physics 2014: efficient blue light-emitting diodes (Akasaki, Amano, Nakamura)
US Department of Energy, LED Lighting Facts and reports on LED lamp lifetime
fiches.corps:
::An LED is a piece of crystal that glows when current flows through it the right way. It replaced the filament bulb in fifteen years, because it makes the same light with ten times less energy.::

## What happens inside

An LED (light-emitting diode) is a **diode**: a component that only lets current through in one direction. At its heart, two layers of semiconductor meet. When current flows, electrons drop from one energy level to another, each releasing a grain of light.

**The colour depends on the material**, not on a filter: red and infrared have existed since the 1960s, efficient blue only arrived in the 1990s, which earned its inventors the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. **A white LED** is a blue LED coated with a yellow powder (a phosphor): blue and yellow mixed look white.

## Useful numbers

**Each colour needs its own voltage**, called the forward voltage:

| Colour | Typical forward voltage |
|---|---|
| Infrared | 1.2 to 1.5 V |
| Red, orange, yellow | 1.8 to 2.2 V |
| Green, blue, white | 2.8 to 3.4 V |

**A small 3 or 5 mm indicator LED** handles about **20 milliamps**. Beyond that, it heats up and dies.

**Direction matters.** The longer leg is plus (the anode). The flat side of the LED's rim is minus (the cathode). Wired backwards, it doesn't light, and beyond a few volts backwards it can burn out.

## The golden rule: always limit the current

An LED connected straight to a battery that's too strong burns out in a fraction of a second: once past its forward voltage, it lets through as much current as it's given. So you put **a resistor in series**, worked out like this:

**R = (source voltage − LED voltage) ÷ desired current**

Example: a white LED (3 V) on a 5 V USB supply, at 20 mA: (5 − 3) ÷ 0.02 = **100 ohms**. When in doubt, take the next value up: the LED will be a little dimmer, and live longer. See [[TEC-ENE-002]].

## Lighting

- **Efficiency**: an LED bulb produces about 100 lumens per watt or more, against 10 to 15 for a filament bulb. For the same light, **ten times less energy**: that's what makes lighting possible on a small battery or a solar panel.
- **Lifetime**: the LEDs themselves last tens of thousands of hours. In a bulb, it's almost always **the power electronics that fail first**, because of heat. An LED bulb shut inside a sealed ceiling fitting lives much shorter.
- **Heat** is the enemy: a power LED must be mounted on a metal heatsink.

## Screens

- **LCD**: LEDs serve as the backlight, see [[TEC-ELN-002]].
- **OLED**: each sub-pixel is a tiny organic LED making its own light. Perfect blacks and infinite contrast, but pixels wear over time and a still image left for months can leave a mark.
- **Giant screens** in stadiums and on buildings: a mosaic of ordinary LEDs, visible in full sun.

## Tinkerer's tips

- **Testing an LED**: a multimeter on diode mode lights it faintly. Or a 3 V button cell, legs pinched on it: a red, green or white LED lights up with no resistor, because the cell can't supply enough current to burn it.
- **Seeing infrared**: a remote control's LED is invisible to the eye, but a phone camera sees it flash purple. It's the quickest remote test there is.
- **An LED bulb that no longer lights** often has just one dead LED in a chain wired in series: a black burnt dot on its surface gives it away. Bridging that LED with a wire sometimes brings the others back. **Careful: these bulbs run straight off 230 volts mains; only touch them unplugged, with the capacitors discharged.**
- **Squeezing the last drop from a spent battery**: a small circuit called a "joule thief" (a transistor, a resistor, a coil wound on a small ferrite ring) boosts the voltage of a half-dead 1.5 V battery to light a white LED for hours.
- **12 V LED strips** can be cut every three LEDs or so, at the marked points. They connect straight to a car or motorbike battery, with no resistor to add: it's already on the strip.

To light an LED without the grid, see [[SURV-ENE-001]] and [[SURV-ENE-002]].

sources: Comiskey B., Albert J., Yoshizawa H., Jacobson J., An electrophoretic ink for all-printed reflective electronic displays, Nature, 1998
E Ink Holdings, datasheets for Carta, Kaleido and Spectra displays
Heikenfeld J. et al., Review Paper: A critical review of the present and future prospects for electronic paper, Journal of the SID, 2011
fiches.corps:
::An e-reader with a dead battery still shows its last page. A screen that keeps its picture without power is exactly what a device built to last needs.::

## The principle

The screen is filled with **microcapsules** thinner than a hair. Each holds a clear liquid and thousands of **pigment particles**: white ones charged one way, black ones charged the other.

Electrodes above and below each dot create an electric field. Depending on its direction, it pulls the white or the black particles to the surface. The dot turns white or black. This is **electrophoresis**, the movement of charged particles in a liquid.

The invention came out of MIT in the late 1990s; the company E Ink industrialised it, and the first consumer e-reader used it in 2004.

## What makes it unique

**It is bistable.** Once moved, the particles stay where they are, without power. The screen only uses energy **while the picture changes**. A page displayed for a week costs nothing.

**It is reflective.** Like paper, it bounces ambient light back. It reads perfectly in full sun, from every angle, and tires the eyes less than a lit screen. In the dark, it needs a front light: a row of LEDs along the edge lighting the surface from above.

## Its limits

- **Slow**: a picture changes in a few tenths of a second. No video, jerky animations.
- **Ghosting**: the previous picture leaves a faint trace. The screen regularly "cleans" itself by flashing all black then all white: that flash is normal.
- **Cold**: below about 0 °C (32 °F), the liquid thickens and picture changes become slow or incomplete. Many displays are rated for 0 to 50 °C. **The picture already shown, however, stays.**
- **Colour** exists in two versions: with colour filters over the black-and-white screen (pale colours, fast), or with pigments of several colours in each capsule (vivid colours, but a picture change takes several seconds).
- **Price**: for the same size, more expensive than an LCD.

## Where you find it

- E-readers and some writing tablets.
- **Electronic shelf labels** in supermarkets: each one is a small electronic ink display with a button cell that lasts years, updated by radio.
- Timetable displays at some solar-powered bus stops.
- Watches and badges with very long battery life.

## Why it's the survival screen

A reading device that must work for weeks far from any socket has three needs: use almost nothing, be readable in daylight, and **show something even when its battery is empty**. Electronic ink is the only technology that ticks all three. That's why it is considered for offline reading devices, see [[TEC-IDE-009]].

## Tips

- **A dead e-reader keeps its last page**: if you leave a map, a list of frequencies or an emergency sheet on it before it dies, the information stays readable.
- **A screen frozen halfway** after a cold snap often recovers if you warm it against your body, then force a full refresh.
- **For a build**, electronic ink modules from 1.5 to 7.5 inches driven over SPI cost from about ten to a few tens of euros. You send the whole picture, then let the screen refresh, often 2 to 15 seconds depending on the model.
- **Don't leave an electronic ink screen in full sun behind a window**: heat and ultraviolet eventually yellow and damage the capsules.

sources: Yang D.-K., Wu S.-T., Fundamentals of Liquid Crystal Devices, Wiley, 2nd edition
Chen J., Cranton W., Fihn M. (eds.), Handbook of Visual Display Technology, Springer
Castellano J., Liquid Gold: The Story of Liquid Crystal Displays and the Creation of an Industry, World Scientific
fiches.corps:
::An LCD makes no light. It's a lamp, and in front of it, millions of shutters opening and closing. Everything you see, you see through them.::

## The principle in three layers

**Light from a lamp** first passes through a **polarizer**: a filter that only lets through light vibrating in one direction.

**Liquid crystals**, sandwiched between two glass plates, have a strange property: their rod-shaped molecules line up on their own, and by lining up in a spiral, they **rotate** the direction of the light passing through them. Apply a small voltage and the molecules stand up straight and stop rotating it.

**A second polarizer**, crossed with the first, only lets through light that has been rotated.

Result: with no voltage, the light rotates and passes, the dot is bright. With voltage, it no longer rotates and is blocked by the second filter, the dot is dark. By adjusting the voltage, you get every shade of grey.

**Colour** comes from tiny red, green and blue filters in front of each sub-pixel. A colour LCD lets through, at best, about a tenth of its lamp's light: the rest is absorbed by the filters and polarizers.

## The families

- **Segment LCDs**: the digits of a calculator, a watch, a thermostat. No lamp, a mirror behind: they are reflective and use a few millionths of a watt.
- **Passive matrix**: old monochrome screens on phones and appliances. Simple, slow, low contrast.
- **Active matrix (TFT)**: a transistor behind each sub-pixel holds its voltage between refreshes. The screen of almost every computer, TV and non-OLED phone.
- **TN, VA, IPS**: three ways of arranging the crystals. TN is fast and cheap but shifts colour as soon as you look from the side; IPS keeps its colours from every angle; VA gives the deepest blacks.

## The backlight

Recent screens are lit by **LEDs**, often placed along one edge: a plastic plate guides the light and spreads it over the whole surface. Screens from before about 2010 used thin **fluorescent tubes** (CCFL), which contain a little mercury and need high voltage to start.

## What damages it

- **Pressure**: pressing hard crushes the crystals and leaves blotches, sometimes permanently.
- **Cold**: below about −20 °C (−4 °F), the crystals turn sluggish and the picture smears. It comes back as it warms up.
- **Strong heat**: a dashboard screen in full sun can turn black. Above a certain temperature, the crystals become an ordinary liquid and lose their effect. That comes back too, as it cools.
- **Dead or stuck pixels**: a failed transistor leaves a dot that is always black or always lit.

## Tips from people who've taken them apart

- **Black screen, device on?** Shine a torch at the screen at an angle, close up. If the picture appears, faintly, only the backlight is dead: the device can still be used to recover data or read a setting.
- **LCD light is polarized.** With polarized sunglasses, a screen can go black when you tilt your head 90 degrees. It isn't broken.
- **The back panel of a broken laptop screen** (the light guide and its LEDs) makes an even, flat light panel, ideal for lighting a room or a workbench, or for tracing. Its LEDs are often wired in series: they need the voltage they were designed for, see [[TEC-ELN-004]].
- **Polarizer sheets** peel off a dead screen. Two crossed sheets show the stresses in clear plastic as rainbows, and a single one works as a polarizing filter for photos.
- **A broken old screen with fluorescent tubes**: don't breathe the dust of shattered tubes, air the room, pick up without a vacuum cleaner.
- **For a build**, small 2 to 3 inch colour LCD modules driven over SPI (ILI9341, ST7789 controllers) cost a few euros and are documented everywhere.

sources: Chen J., Cranton W., Fihn M. (eds.), Handbook of Visual Display Technology, Springer, 2nd edition
Society for Information Display, Display Technology Guide
E Ink Holdings, technical documentation on electrophoretic displays
fiches.parcours: Lisez d'abord cette fiche, qui explique ce qu'ont en commun tous les écrans. Le chapitre sur l'écran à cristaux liquides couvre presque tout ce que vous avez sous la main ; celui sur l'encre électronique explique pourquoi c'est l'écran des appareils qui doivent tenir des semaines sur une pile.
fiches.corps:
::A screen doesn't show a picture. It lights up, switches off or masks millions of tiny dots fast enough for the eye to take them for a picture.::

This subject reads in three parts: this sheet, which explains what all screens share, then two chapters, [[TEC-ELN-002]] on liquid crystals and [[TEC-ELN-003]] on electronic ink. LEDs, which light most screens and make up some on their own, have their own sheet: [[TEC-ELN-004]].

## The pixel

Every screen is a grid of **pixels**. On a colour screen, each pixel is made of three **sub-pixels**, red, green and blue. By setting the brightness of each, you get every colour: all three at full give white, all three off give black.

**Resolution** is the number of pixels: 1920 × 1080 for "Full HD", 3840 × 2160 for 4K. **Density** is pixels per inch (ppi): beyond about 300 ppi at phone reading distance, the eye can no longer tell the dots apart.

The same number of pixels looks sharp on a phone and coarse on a big TV: density decides sharpness, not resolution alone.

## Three ways of making light

Every screen falls into one of these families.

| Family | Principle | Examples | In sunlight | In the dark |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Emissive | Each dot makes its own light | OLED, giant LED walls, old tube TVs, plasma | Average | Perfect |
| Transmissive | A lamp behind, shutters in front | Computer, TV and phone LCD screens | Average to poor | Good |
| Reflective | No lamp: they bounce back ambient light, like paper | Electronic ink, calculator and watch LCDs | Perfect | Unreadable without a light |

**This table decides power use.** An emissive or transmissive screen spends energy every second it is on, and the backlight is often the biggest drain in a phone or a laptop. A reflective screen uses almost nothing: an LCD calculator runs for years on a button cell, an e-reader for weeks.

## Refreshing the picture

A computer screen redraws its picture 60 times a second or more (60 Hz, 120 Hz). That's what makes motion smooth. An electronic ink screen only changes the picture when told to, and takes a fraction of a second to do it: perfect for a page, useless for video.

## How a screen gets the picture

- **Large screens** receive the picture through a video cable: HDMI, DisplayPort, and older VGA (analogue, still very common on old monitors and projectors).
- **Small screens** in electronic devices are driven directly by a small controller, through a serial link with a few wires (SPI, I2C) or a parallel bus. This is what you use to build a device yourself with a microcontroller, see [[TEC-IDE-009]].
- **The controller** is a chip bonded behind the panel, which keeps the picture in memory and redraws it on its own. Each model has its own commands: without its documentation, a salvaged screen is very hard to bring to life.

## What you learn by taking them apart

- **Old phone screens are hard to reuse.** Their connectors have pins 0.4 mm apart or less, their controller often has no public documentation, and their backlight sometimes needs more than 10 volts. For a build, a screen module sold for microcontrollers, already mounted on a small board, costs a few euros and saves days.
- **A broken laptop screen** contains a flat, diffusing light panel behind the liquid crystals: an excellent lighting panel once powered. See [[TEC-ELN-002]].
- **A screen that stays black** isn't necessarily dead: often only the backlight has failed. Shine a torch at the screen at an angle, and the picture appears.
- **Touchscreens** are one more layer, glued in front of the panel: you can crack a phone's touch glass without harming the display, and the other way round.

fiches.corps:
::A punctured tyre is almost never a lost tyre. A nail in the tread is fixed in ten minutes at the roadside. Driving on it flat, on the other hand, kills it within a few hundred metres.::

## UNDERSTAND

**What can be fixed**: a hole in the **tread**, the part that touches the ground, up to about 6 mm. A nail, a screw, a shard.

**What can't**: the **sidewall** (the side), the shoulder (the curve between sidewall and tread), a long cut, a tyre that has been driven flat. The sidewall flexes on every turn: a repair won't hold there.

**Driving flat** crushes the sidewall between rim and road: it heats up and tears inside, and the tyre is scrap, even if it looks fine from outside. **Stop as soon as you feel the car pull or thump.** How a tyre is built is explained in [[TEC-MEC-010]].

## ACT

### Find the leak

- **Look** at the tread while rolling the car a few centimetres: a nail, a screw head, a shiny shard.
- **Listen**: a hiss.
- **Soapy water** brushed or poured on: bubbles where it leaks. Check the valve and the rim edge too.

### Fixing a tubeless car tyre: the plug

A plug kit (a few euros in any car shop) makes the strongest repair you can do yourself.

1. **Leave the nail in** until you're ready: it's plugging the hole.
2. Pull it out with pliers.
3. **Ream the hole** with the kit's rasp tool, pushing it in and twisting several times: it cleans the hole and sizes it.
4. Thread a sticky plug string halfway through the eye of the insertion needle.
5. Push the needle in until only one to two centimetres of string stay outside.
6. **Pull the needle out in one sharp move**, without twisting: the string stays in the hole.
7. Cut off the excess flush, reinflate, check with soapy water.

It's a roadside repair: have the tyre checked by a professional as soon as possible, who will fit a patch from the inside.

### The sealant can

It reinflates and plugs small holes in minutes. It gets you going, but it gums up the valve and the pressure sensor, and many garages then refuse to repair the tyre. Drive gently to the garage.

### Changing the wheel

1. Car on flat ground, handbrake on, in gear, passengers well away from the road.
2. **Loosen the nuts a quarter turn with the wheel on the ground**, before lifting: otherwise the wheel spins in the air.
3. Put the jack on the proper point (a notch under the sill, shown in the manual), lift until the wheel clears the ground.
4. Unscrew, swap the wheel, screw on by hand, **then tighten in a star pattern** (one nut, the one opposite, and so on).
5. Lower the car, tighten fully. **Retighten after 50 km (30 miles).**

A narrow space-saver spare is limited to 80 km/h (50 mph) and meant for getting home.

### Fixing an inner tube (bike, wheelbarrow, old two-wheelers)

1. Take out the tube, inflate it a little, find the hole (in water, bubbles; otherwise by ear or against your cheek).
2. Sand around the hole with the kit's sandpaper.
3. Spread the glue a little wider than the patch, and **wait until it's dry to the touch**, three to five minutes. It's everyone's mistake: a patch pressed onto wet glue won't hold.
4. Apply the patch, press hard for a minute.
5. **Before refitting, find the cause**: run your fingers gently around the inside of the tyre. A forgotten thorn punctures the new tube within a mile.

## ADAPT

**The tyre has come off the rim.** To reinflate it, the beads must touch the rim. Tighten a **ratchet strap** around the tread: it squeezes the tyre and pushes the beads outwards. Wet the edges with soapy water, inflate, then release the strap as soon as the beads snap into place. The trick with petrol or spray set alight inside the tyre exists: it burns hands and bursts tyres, don't touch it.

**A cut in the sidewall of a bike tyre.** Slip a piece of old tyre, a folded energy-bar wrapper or a banknote inside, between tyre and tube: it stops the tube bulging through the slit, long enough to get home.

**No patch left.** For a bike: cut the tube at the hole and **tie a knot** with the two ends. The shorter tube goes back in and holds. For anything else: very tight tape, several turns, for a few kilometres.

**No tube, nothing.** Stuff the tyre with rope, packed dry grass, foam, old clothes: heavy and hard, but it rolls, slowly, to get you out of trouble. See [[SURV-REC-022]].

**No compressor.** A bike floor pump inflates a car tyre, with a few hundred strokes. A small 12 V compressor plugs into the cigarette lighter. A CO2 cartridge reinflates a bike tyre in two seconds.

**A second-hand tyre found on a wreck**: read its date (four digits after DOT, week and year) and look for cracks on the sidewalls. See [[SURV-REC-003]].

fiches.corps:
::A railway looks like two iron bars laid on stones. It is really a layered structure, designed to carry trains of thousands of tonnes to the millimetre, through rain, frost and heatwaves.::

## The layers, from bottom to top

1. **The formation**: the levelled, compacted, drained ground. A railway starts with earthworks: embankments, cuttings, ditches.
2. **The sub-ballast**: a layer of compacted gravel that spreads the loads and stops the soil working its way up.
3. **The ballast**: crushed stone, hard and angular, about 25 to 50 mm, some thirty centimetres deep. Its angles lock together and hold the sleepers; its gaps let water through. **Round pebbles wouldn't hold anything.**
4. **The sleepers** (ties in North America): concrete today, creosote-treated wood on older lines, sometimes steel. About **1,666 sleepers per kilometre**, 60 cm apart.
5. **The fastenings**: elastic steel clips that press the rail onto the sleeper, with a rubber pad between them. On wood, large screws called coach screws.
6. **The rails**: very hard steel. Main lines use rails of **60 kg per metre**.

## Gauge

The distance between the inner faces of the two rails:

| Gauge | Name | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 1,435 mm | Standard gauge | Western Europe, North America, China, high-speed lines |
| 1,520 mm | Russian broad gauge | Russia, Ukraine, the Baltic states, Finland (1,524) |
| 1,668 mm | Iberian gauge | Spain and Portugal (except high speed) |
| 1,000 mm | Metre gauge | Mountain lines, Africa, Southeast Asia |

At borders where the gauge changes, bogies are swapped, loads are transferred, or variable-gauge wheelsets are used. See [[TEC-MEC-012]].

## Continuous welded rail

Modern rails are no longer laid in lengths with joints: they are **welded end to end over kilometres**, by electric welding in the factory and **thermite welding** on site (a reaction of aluminium powder and iron oxide that produces liquid steel, poured into a mould between the two rails).

A one-kilometre rail would like to grow by almost 50 cm between winter and summer. **It's prevented from doing so**: it's laid under tension, at a chosen temperature, and the ballast and fastenings hold it. In a heatwave, if the track is poorly maintained, it can suddenly kink sideways: that's **buckling**, one of the reasons for summer speed restrictions.

## What you find around it

- **Cant**: in curves, the outer rail is raised, by up to 16 to 18 cm, to tilt the train like a banked bend.
- **Switches** (points): two movable blades that steer the wheels, and a **frog** where the rails cross. Check rails hold the wheelset while it crosses the gap at the frog. The blades are moved by a motor and locked.
- **Signalling**: the line is divided into blocks; electrical circuits in the rails detect a train by its axles, which short the two rails together.
- **Electrification**: in France, **1,500 volts DC** on part of the older network, **25,000 volts AC** on newer and high-speed lines, through overhead catenary.

## Maintenance

**Tamping machines** lift the track, pack the ballast under each sleeper with vibrating tines, and bring the track back to level to the millimetre. Measuring trains run over the network to detect geometry faults and cracks in the rails.

## What railway workers know

- **A train can't stop.** A freight train at 100 km/h (60 mph) needs about a kilometre to stop; a TGV at 300 km/h, more than three kilometres. By the time the driver sees you, it's already too late.
- **The catenary kills without contact.** At 25,000 volts, an arc can strike without contact, simply because someone comes too close. Every year, young people die climbing onto parked wagons. Never climb onto a wagon under overhead wires, even if the train has been standing for days.
- **Rails are slippery**, especially wet or icy: step over them, don't walk on them.
- **A piece of rail is the best improvised anvil** there is: hard, heavy steel with a flat top. Amateur blacksmiths all over the world start this way. See [[TEC-MEC-005]].
- **An abandoned line** is still a route: gentle gradients, bridges, tunnels, and a line that always leads to a station, so to a town. But **a line that looks abandoned isn't always**: listen, look at the rails (shiny on top means they're still in use).

sources: Iwnicki S. (ed.), Handbook of Railway Vehicle Dynamics, CRC Press, 2nd edition
Esveld C., Modern Railway Track, MRT Productions
UIC, technical leaflets on axles, wheels and wheel profiles
fiches.corps:
::A train has no steering wheel. It turns because its wheels are slightly conical, and it takes curves because its wheels sit on carriages that pivot under the body: the bogies.::

## What it is

A **bogie** (called a *truck* in North America) is a carriage with two axles, sometimes three, placed under each end of a coach or locomotive. The body rests on it through a pivot: **the bogie can turn under it**. That's what lets a twenty-metre vehicle follow a curve, while its wheels stay parallel to the rails.

A freight wagon or passenger coach has two bogies, so four axles and eight wheels. A bogie weighs several tonnes.

## The wheelset: why a train turns without steering

**The two wheels of an axle are fixed to the same shaft.** They always turn together, at the same speed. In a curve, the outer wheel has further to travel: how does it manage?

**The tread is conical.** When the wheelset shifts towards the outside of the curve, the outer wheel rolls on a larger diameter and the inner wheel on a smaller one. The outer wheel then covers more ground per turn, and the wheelset centres itself. **That's what guides the train**, far more than the flanges.

**The flange**, the rim on the inside of each wheel, is only a safety: it should only touch the rail in tight curves and at switches. When it rubs, you hear the high screech of trains in curves.

## The suspensions

- **Primary suspension**, between the axle boxes and the bogie frame: metal springs or rubber blocks. It absorbs track defects.
- **Secondary suspension**, between the bogie and the body: often air springs on passenger trains. That's what makes the ride comfortable.

## What goes on a bogie

- **Brakes**: discs on the axle, or blocks rubbing on the tread.
- **Traction motors**, on the powered bogies of locomotives and multiple units. The others are called trailer bogies.
- **Sensors** for speed and axle box temperature, and the beacons of the speed control system.

## Variants

- **The Jacobs bogie** is shared between two cars, at their joint. It's the principle of articulated trainsets like the TGV: fewer bogies, a more stable and lighter train.
- **Variable-gauge bogies** change the distance between their wheels while rolling slowly through a special installation, to pass from one network to another, between Spain and France for example.
- **Trams and metros** have smaller bogies for much tighter curves.

## Tips from people who maintain them

- **Hunting**: above a certain speed, a conical wheelset swings left and right more and more. The whole design of a high-speed bogie aims to damp it. A worn bogie that "hunts" is felt in the body as a regular sway.
- **Wheels are reprofiled** without being removed: the train rolls over an underfloor lathe that shaves the tread back to its conical profile.
- **A "flat" on a wheel**, made when the wheel skidded locked under braking, makes a regular hammering noise: the famous "clack-clack-clack" of a train arriving with a damaged wheel.
- **Axle boxes** heat up when their bearing is dying. Trackside detectors measure their temperature as trains pass, and stop the train before the axle breaks.

The track all this rolls on is described in [[TEC-MEC-013]].

fiches.corps:
::In a petrol engine, everything starts with a spark lasting a few thousandths of a second. The plug that makes it also tells you, by its colour, how the engine is doing.::

## Its job

A petrol engine draws in a mix of air and fuel, compresses it, then **ignites it at the right moment**: the spark plug does that, dozens of times a second. How the whole engine works is in [[TEC-MOTH-001]].

**A diesel engine has no spark plugs.** Diesel ignites on its own from the heat of compression. Its "glow plugs" are small heaters that warm the chamber to help cold starts: a completely different object.

## What's inside

- **The terminal**, at the top, where the lead or coil connects.
- **The insulator**, in white ceramic: it stops the current escaping before the tip.
- **The metal shell**, with its thread and hex: it screws into the cylinder head and makes the earth.
- **The centre electrode** and **the ground electrode**, separated by a small space, **the gap**, about 0.6 to 1.1 mm depending on the engine.

The **ignition coil** turns the battery's 12 volts into **20,000 to 40,000 volts**. At that voltage, the current jumps the gap as a spark and ignites the mixture.

**Materials** decide how long it lasts: a standard plug with a nickel electrode lasts about 20,000 to 30,000 km; a platinum or iridium-tipped plug, 60,000 to 100,000 km.

**The heat range** says whether the plug sheds heat fast ("cold" plug, for high-performance engines) or slowly ("hot" plug). **Always fit the one the manufacturer specifies**: a plug that's too hot can melt a piston.

## Reading a plug

Unscrewed, a plug shows how the engine burns.

| What the tip looks like | What it means |
|---|---|
| Light grey to tan | All is well |
| Black, dry, powdery (soot) | Mixture too rich, clogged air filter, weak spark, too much idling |
| Black, wet and oily | Oil is getting into the chamber: worn rings or seals |
| Wet with fuel | Flooded engine: too much fuel and no spark when starting |
| White, blistered, eroded electrodes | Overheating: mixture too lean or plug too hot. Fix it fast |
| Glassy yellow or green deposits | Additives or poor-quality fuel |

## A mechanic's tips

- **Checking the spark**: unscrew the plug, reconnect it to its lead, rest its shell against a metal part of the engine, and crank the starter. A **blue, crisp** spark: ignition is fine. Yellow and weak, or nothing: coil, lead or plug. **Hold the lead by its insulating boot**, never the plug with a bare hand: the shock hurts.
- **Flooded engine** (smell of fuel, it coughs but won't catch): on a modern car, floor the throttle while cranking and the injection cuts fuel to clear the excess. On a mower or chainsaw, unscrew the plug, dry it, pull the starter several times with the plug out to blow out the fuel, refit.
- **Tightening**: by hand until it seats, then about half a turn with the wrench for a new plug with a gasket. Too tight and you strip the thread in the aluminium head; too loose and it overheats and works loose.
- **Start the thread by hand** for several turns so it doesn't cross-thread. A short piece of rubber hose pushed onto the plug helps guide it in straight at the bottom of a deep plug well.
- **A spare plug** and its wrench belong in the kit of every chainsaw, brush cutter or trail bike. On a two-stroke engine they foul much faster.
- **The gap is adjusted** by gently bending the ground electrode, and measured with a feeler gauge. In a pinch, a bank card is about 0.76 mm thick.

An engine that won't start is diagnosed step by step in [[SURV-REC-019]].

fiches.corps:
::A tyre holds a car weighing a tonne and a half on four patches the size of a postcard. Everything it's made of serves to keep those four postcards stuck to the road.::

## What's inside

A tyre isn't a block of rubber. It's an assembly of layers, each with a job.

- **The tread**: the rubber that touches the ground, with grooves that clear water away.
- **The belt**: two layers of crossed steel cords under the tread. They stiffen it and keep it flat.
- **The carcass**: textile cords (polyester, rayon) embedded in rubber, running from one edge to the other. It's the tyre's frame.
- **The sidewalls**: the sides, flexible, soaking up shocks. They're thin: this is the fragile part.
- **The beads**: two rings of braided steel wire that press the tyre onto the rim and stop it jumping off.
- **The inner liner**: a layer of butyl rubber, almost airtight. It's what replaces the inner tube in a "tubeless" tyre.

## Radial or bias-ply

In a **radial tyre**, the carcass cords run straight from one bead to the other, like spokes, and the steel belt holds the tread. The sidewall flexes, the tread stays flat: better grip, less heat, longer life. Michelin patented it in 1946 and sold it from the end of the 1940s; today it's on almost every car.

In a **bias-ply tyre**, older, the cords cross diagonally. It's still used on some farm machinery, trailers and classic motorbikes.

## The rubber

- **Natural rubber**, tapped from the rubber tree, and synthetic rubbers made from oil.
- **Carbon black**: this is what makes tyres black. It strengthens them and protects them from ultraviolet.
- **Silica**, in recent tyres, which improves wet grip and lowers rolling resistance.
- **Sulphur**: heated with the rubber, it links its molecules together. That's **vulcanisation**, discovered by Charles Goodyear in 1839. Without it, rubber gets sticky in the heat and brittle in the cold.

## Making one

The layers are built up flat on a drum, forming a soft "green" tyre. It then goes into a heated press, around 150 to 180 °C: a mould stamps its tread pattern and markings while the rubber vulcanises, in about ten minutes for a car tyre.

## Reading a sidewall

Example: **205/55 R16 91V**

| Marking | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 205 | Width, in millimetres |
| 55 | Sidewall height, as a percentage of the width |
| R | Radial |
| 16 | Rim diameter, in inches |
| 91 | Load index: 615 kg (1,356 lb) per tyre |
| V | Speed rating: 240 km/h (149 mph) maximum |

**The date of manufacture**: a four-digit code in an oval, after the letters DOT. **2319** means the 23rd week of 2019.

**Winter tyres** carry the symbol of a three-peaked mountain with a snowflake (3PMSF). The M+S marking alone means "mud and snow", without guaranteeing real performance on snow.

## What wears it and what kills it

- **Under-inflation**: the sidewall flexes too much on every turn, heats up and eventually bursts. It's the leading cause of tyre destruction. The recommended pressure is on a label in the door frame or the fuel flap, and is measured **cold**.
- **Age**: even with little use, rubber hardens and cracks. Cracks on the sidewalls or between the tread blocks: it's time to replace it, whatever its depth. Generally count 6 to 10 years at most.
- **Wear**: European law requires at least **1.6 mm** of tread. Wear indicators, small bars at the bottom of the grooves, come level at that depth.
- **Driving on a flat**, even for a few hundred metres, destroys the inside of the sidewall. See [[SURV-REC-024]].

## Tips from people who fit them every day

- **A one-euro coin** slipped into a groove: if its gold rim shows, there's more than about 3 mm left. Less, and the tyre is tired on wet roads. (In the US, the same test uses a penny and Lincoln's head.)
- **A tyre that loses a little air every week** often has a nail in the tread, or a corroded rim leaking at the bead. Soapy water bubbles where it leaks.
- **Aircraft tyres** are inflated with nitrogen: no moisture, no oxygen, no fire if they overheat.
- **An old tyre is a resource**: sandal soles (Vietnamese soldiers walked on them), earth-filled retaining walls, protection, bumpers. **Burned, it gives off toxic black smoke** and oils that pollute the soil: never use it as fuel.

fiches.corps:
::A tool can be found, a book can be read, but a skill learned over twenty years can't be replaced. In a crisis, what runs out first isn't equipment. It's people who know how to use it.::

## Why trades matter

A modern society spreads knowledge across thousands of trades. Each person only knows a small part of what keeps them alive, and it all works because others know the rest. When exchange stops, a group is only worth **what its members can do with their hands**.

What follows says, trade by trade, **what they know that you don't**. Each trade will get its own sheet over time.

## Caring

- **Nurse**: injections, drips, dressings, watching a patient day and night, spotting when things get worse. **The most useful trade day to day** in a group, even more than the doctor, because most care is care that lasts.
- **Doctor**: diagnosis, choice of treatment, technical procedures.
- **Midwife**: pregnancies, births, newborns. Knowledge that saves two lives at once. See [[URG-SEC-007]].
- **Pharmacist**: which drug replaces which, doses, interactions, what keeps and what expires.
- **Vet**: surgery, anaesthesia, antibiotics, on patients who can't talk. They know much of what a doctor knows, and they're used to making do with little.
- **Dentist**: toothache makes an adult useless within two days.
- **Physiotherapist**: immobilising, rehabilitating, relieving a back.
- **Firefighter, first aider, paramedic**: the first minutes, the injured, fire, transport.

## Building and maintaining

- **Plumber**: water in and water out. Without them, disease comes fast. See [[TEC-CON-006]].
- **Electrician**: wiring without killing anyone, connecting a generator or solar panels properly. See [[TEC-ENE-003]].
- **Heating engineer**: stoves, flues, gas, and the carbon monoxide that kills people who heat badly.
- **Mason, carpenter, roofer**: a watertight roof before winter, a wall that stands. The roofer is the one you notice missing at the first rain.
- **Mechanic**: engines, pumps, generators, vehicles. Also the most resourceful with parts that aren't the right ones.
- **Welder, metalworker, blacksmith**: repairing what broke, making what can't be found any more.
- **Electronics technician, phone and radio repairer**: bringing devices back, communicating. See [[SIG-COM-002]].

## Feeding

- **Farmer, market gardener, livestock keeper**: producing food season after season. The knowledge that takes longest to acquire, and the one people most regret not having. See [[TEC-AGR-001]] and [[TEC-ELE-001]].
- **Baker**: sourdough, the wood oven, bread for a hundred people.
- **Butcher, charcutier**: slaughtering, cutting, salting, smoking, wasting nothing of an animal. See [[TEC-ELE-007]].
- **Miller, beekeeper, fisher, hunter, forager**: each a whole branch of food.
- **Canteen or army cook**: feeding many people, every day, with whatever there is, without poisoning anyone.

## Making

- **Seamstress, tailor, cobbler**: clothes and shoes that last. See [[TEC-MAT-005]].
- **Joiner, cabinetmaker**: furniture, tools, handles, carts.
- **Potter, basket maker, tanner, soap maker, brewer**: forgotten trades that become precious again as soon as the shelves empty.

## Organising and passing on

- **Teacher**: so children keep learning, and knowledge gets passed on.
- **Stock manager, logistician, bookkeeper**: knowing what you have, what you use, and how long it will last.
- **Radio amateur**: talking far away without a network.
- **Soldier, police officer, security guard**: guard duty, discipline, tense situations.
- **Psychologist, social worker, mediator**: holding a group together when everyone is at the end of their rope. See [[SURV-PSY-003]].

## Taking stock of a group's skills

1. **Don't ask "what's your job?", ask "what can you do with your hands?"** An accountant may be a passionate gardener; a retired nurse may be the best seamstress in the neighbourhood.
2. **Count hobbies**: hunting, fishing, gardening, DIY, sewing, radio, hiking, volunteer first aid.
3. **Note the tools** each person owns, and **what they're willing to teach**.
4. **Pair an apprentice with each person who knows**: knowledge carried by one person disappears with them.

## What people who rebuilt know

- **Retired people are a goldmine.** Many learned their trade without computers, with hand tools, and know how to fix what younger people replace.
- **Maintenance trades are missed before prestigious ones.** A town lasts longer without a banker than without a plumber.
- **A skill is currency.** In a trade, an hour of a roofer's or a dentist's time is worth more than many objects. See [[SURV-TROC-001]].
- **A skill is learned by watching someone do it, then doing it under someone's eye**, not from a book. Phenix sheets give the map; apprenticeship is the ground. See [[SURV-SOC-001]].

fiches.corps:
::In French, one word, "cintre", covers the wire hanger in your wardrobe, the timber frame that held up every stone vault in the world while it was being built, and the plumber's trick for bending a pipe without crushing it. All three are useful.::

## The clothes hanger

**Its history.** Wooden supports for clothes have existed for a long time; a first American patent for a wire garment hook dates from 1869. The modern shape, a wire triangle with a hook, is credited to **Albert Parkhouse**, a Michigan worker who, the story goes, bent a wire to hang his coat on in 1903 because every coat hook was taken.

**Its materials**

- **Steel wire**, about 2 to 3 mm, often galvanised, painted or plastic-coated: the dry cleaner's hanger. One hanger gives a little over a metre of wire once straightened.
- **Wood**, for suits and coats, because it keeps the shape of the shoulders.
- **Plastic**, light and cheap, which snaps in the cold.

## The wire hanger: a resource

A metre of stiff steel wire that bends by hand and keeps its shape. People who carry them make:

- **a hook** to hang a pot over the fire, a bag out of reach of rodents, a lamp from a tent roof;
- **a grilling skewer**: first burn off the paint or plastic in the flames, down to bare metal, before putting food on it;
- **a drain snake** to clear a trap: a hook at the end, and you pull the hair out instead of pushing it in;
- **a makeshift antenna** for an FM radio or a TV, plugged into the antenna socket: a straightened, raised wire picks up far better than nothing, see [[TEC-RAD-001]];
- **a reinforcing splint** for a finger or wrist, well padded, see [[URG-FRAC-001]];
- **a "third hand"** to hold two wires while soldering, or a light aimed at an engine;
- **a binding** to tighten a split handle, a hose, a dangling exhaust.

**What it doesn't do well**: fish hooks (too thick and too soft to hold a decent fish) and snares (too stiff to close). For those, fine brass or annealed steel wire is far better.

## The mason's centring: how a vault is built

A stone vault or arch **only stands once it's finished**: until the top stone, the **keystone**, is in place, the stones fall inwards. During construction, they rest on a **centring**: a temporary timber frame cut exactly to the shape of the vault.

1. The centring is raised on props, with **wedges** underneath.
2. The stones (the **voussoirs**) are laid on each side, rising symmetrically.
3. The keystone goes in at the top. All the stones press against each other.
4. The centring is **struck**: the wedges are eased out, the centring drops a few centimetres, and the vault starts carrying itself.

Roman bridges, cathedrals, vaulted cellars: all were built on centrings. A well-made vault works only in compression, which is why stone bridges without mortar have stood for two thousand years. See [[TEC-CON-001]].

## Bending a pipe: bend it without crushing it

Bending a copper or steel pipe by hand flattens it at the bend, and water no longer flows. Plumbers **bend** it properly:

- with a **pipe bender**, a grooved wheel the pipe is wrapped around;
- with a **bending spring**, slid inside or around the pipe, which keeps it from collapsing;
- and with nothing, **using sand**: plug one end, fill the pipe with dry sand packed tight, plug the other, then bend slowly around a post or a round log. The sand supports the wall. Annealed copper (heated to dull red then cooled) bends even more easily.

## Theatre flies

Above a stage, the **fly tower** (in French, *les cintres*) is the upper part of the stage house, where scenery, curtains and lights are raised, hung from battens and counterweights. The stagehands who work there, the flymen, inherited their craft directly from ship rigging: sailors largely invented the job, and their knots are the knots of sailing ships. See [[SURV-NOE-001]].

::Nothing caught fire, nobody smoked, not a spark. And yet the pile of rags in the garage is burning at three in the morning. Spontaneous combustion isn't magic: it's heat building up faster than it can escape.::

## The mechanism

Some materials **heat up on their own**, slowly: they oxidise in contact with air, or bacteria make them ferment. In a small, well-aired volume, this heat escapes and nothing happens.

But in **a pile**, a bag, a tightly packed bale, **the heat stays trapped in the middle**. The hotter it gets, the faster the reaction goes, so the hotter it gets. After a few hours or a few weeks, the core reaches its **self-ignition** temperature, and fire starts from the inside, with no outside flame.

Three conditions, always the same: **a material that heats itself, a volume large enough to hold the heat, and just enough air.**

## Real cases, from most to least common

**Rags soaked in drying oil.** Linseed oil, teak oil, some stains and oil-based varnishes dry by absorbing oxygen from the air, and that reaction gives off heat. A rag balled up in a bin can ignite within hours. It's one of the best-known causes of fire for firefighters in workshops, building sites and garages.

**Hay stored too damp.** Above about 20% moisture, the bacteria in the hay ferment and heat the bale or the loft. The temperature climbs for days, then chemical reactions take over. Barns burn this way one to six weeks after haymaking.

**Piles of compost, manure, sawdust, wood chips and coal.** Large industrial piles are monitored with temperature probes.

**Some metal powders and chemical residues** ignite in air as soon as they come out of their packaging: they're called **pyrophoric**. That's the case with iron sulphide deposits in old oil tanks, which are opened with great care.

**Damaged lithium batteries**: an internal short makes them heat up until they run away. It isn't spontaneous combustion in the strict sense, but the result is the same, with no visible cause.

## Spontaneous human combustion: myth and reality

The story has come back since the 18th century: a person is found almost entirely reduced to ash in a barely blackened room, feet or hands intact. It was long called spontaneous human combustion.

**Today's accepted explanation is the wick effect.** An ordinary heat source (a cigarette, a heater, a candle) sets fire to the clothes of a person who can no longer react: asleep, drunk, ill, already dead. Body fat melts, soaks into the clothing like a candle wick, and burns slowly for hours, with a small flame that barely spreads around it. Experiments with clothed pig carcasses have reproduced it. **No case has shown a body catching fire without an outside source.**

## A few temperatures worth knowing

| Material | Self-ignites at about |
|---|---|
| Paper | 230 °C (Ray Bradbury's famous 451 °F) |
| Wood | 250 to 300 °C depending on species and exposure time |
| Diesel | 210 to 250 °C |
| Petrol | 250 to 300 °C |

**Diesel self-ignites at a lower temperature than petrol**, even though it's much less volatile. That's what makes the diesel engine work: it ignites fuel by the heat of compression alone.

## Firefighters' tips

- **An oily rag** never goes balled up in a bin. Spread it flat outside until it's dry and stiff, or drop it into a closed metal can full of water.
- **A haystack that smokes or smells of caramel, tobacco or burning**: don't open it, don't move it. The fresh air getting in would make the fire smouldering at the core flare up. Push a metal bar into the middle and leave it a few minutes: if it's too hot to hold, call the fire brigade.
- **A compost heap that steams in winter** is normal. A compost heap that turns black in the middle and smells burnt is too big and too dry: spread it out.
- **Sunlight through a water bottle, a jar or a make-up mirror** can focus onto a curtain, a pile of paper or a dry hedge: not spontaneous, but it looks like it, and it surprises people every summer. It's also a way to light a fire, see [[SURV-FEU-002]].
- **A swollen phone or scooter battery** comes out of the house and goes on a non-flammable surface, outdoors if possible.

What to do about a fire that has started: [[URG-INC-001]] and [[URG-INC-002]].

fiches.corps:
::A fruit is sugary water in a skin, with just enough vitamins for an animal to want to eat it and scatter its seeds further away. We are that animal.::

## What's inside

**Water, mostly**: 80 to 90% of the weight of fresh fruit. Watermelon and strawberries exceed 90%, an apple is about 86%, a banana 75%.

**Sugars**: fructose, glucose and sucrose, depending on the fruit. They provide most of its energy.

**Fibre**, including **pectin**, which makes jam set.

**Acids**: citric (citrus), malic (apple), tartaric (grape). They make fruit tart, and they're what allows fruit to be bottled without risk of botulism, see [[TEC-ALI-005]].

**Vitamins and minerals**: vitamin C above all, potassium, and, in orange fruit, pigments the body turns into vitamin A.

**Very little protein and almost no fat**, with exceptions: avocado, olive, coconut.

## Useful numbers (per 100 g of fresh fruit)

| Fruit | Energy | Vitamin C | What sets it apart |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apple | 52 kcal | 5 mg | Keeps for months in the cool |
| Banana | 89 kcal | 9 mg | Rich in potassium (358 mg) |
| Orange | 47 kcal | 53 mg | Travels well |
| Kiwi | 61 kcal | 93 mg | One of the best sources of vitamin C |
| Strawberry | 32 kcal | 59 mg | Very little pectin |
| Blackcurrant | 63 kcal | 181 mg | Europe's champion |
| Guava | 68 kcal | 228 mg | The tropics' champion |
| Grape | 69 kcal | 3 mg | Lots of sugar, few vitamins |
| Avocado | 160 kcal | 10 mg | 15 g of fat: the most filling |
| Dried date | 282 kcal | 0 mg | Concentrated energy, keeps for years |
| Dried apricot | 241 kcal | 1 mg | Concentrated iron and potassium |

**Vitamin C** is the reason fruit matters in hard times. About **10 mg a day** is enough to prevent scurvy; recommendations for good health are around 100 mg. It is **destroyed by heat, air and time**: cooked or dried fruit loses a large part of it.

## What's toxic

- **The kernels inside the stones** of apricots, peaches, plums and cherries, and apple pips, contain **amygdalin**, which releases cyanide when crushed or chewed. Swallowed whole by accident, they pass through. **Bitter apricot kernels**, sometimes sold as a "remedy", poison a child in small numbers.
- **Black elder**: raw berries, leaves and stems cause nausea. Fully ripe berries are eaten **cooked** (jam, syrup).
- **Rhubarb leaves** are rich in oxalic acid. Only the stalks are eaten.
- **Grapefruit** interferes with how many medicines are cleared (some for cholesterol, blood pressure, anxiety) and can push their level in the blood too high. If you take a treatment, check the leaflet.
- **An unknown wild fruit** isn't tasted: see [[SURV-COM-001]].

## Ripening

Some fruits keep ripening after picking, because they give off a gas, **ethylene**, which speeds up their own ripening and their neighbours': **banana, apple, pear, avocado, tomato, mango, kiwi**. Others stop ripening once picked: **citrus, grape, strawberry, cherry, pineapple**.

## Tips from people who store them

- **To ripen a hard avocado or kiwi**, shut it in a paper bag with a ripe banana or apple: the ethylene does the job in a day or two.
- **To keep apples for months**, choose sound ones, unbruised, picked by hand. Store them one by one, not touching, in the cool (1 to 5 °C), in a damp cellar. **Remove any that start to rot every week**: one bad apple speeds up all the others. And keep them away from potatoes and carrots, which ethylene makes sprout or taste bitter.
- **Rose hips**, the red fruit of the dog rose, stay on hedges all winter and contain several hundred milligrams of vitamin C per 100 g. They were Britain's vitamin C reserve during the war. Eat them as syrup or jam, without the hairs around the seeds, which are very irritating.
- **Drying fruit** concentrates its sugar and energy: it takes about 5 to 7 kg of fresh apricots for 1 kg of dried ones. See [[TEC-ALI-003]].
- **Pectin-rich fruit** (apple, quince, redcurrant, citrus peel) sets the jams of fruit that lack it (strawberry, cherry): a few chopped apples in the pot are enough.

## A little botany

To a botanist, a fruit is whatever holds the seeds. Tomato, pepper, cucumber and aubergine are therefore fruits; banana and avocado are berries. And the strawberry isn't really one at all: its flesh is the flower's receptacle, and its true fruits are the little seeds on its surface.

fiches.corps:
::Against a wildfire, you don't win by running. You win by deciding early, getting behind something solid for the few minutes the front takes to pass, then putting out the embers it leaves behind.::

## ACT

### 1. Raise the alarm, right now

**112** (or your local emergency number, 18 for firefighters in France, 911 in North America), even for a fire that looks tiny. Give the most precise location you can: road, place name, visible landmark, direction of the smoke. A fire reported in the first minutes is almost always stopped.

### 2. A small fire, at your feet

You can attack it **if the flames stay lower than your knees and you have a way out behind you**:

- attack it **from the rear or the flanks**, never from the front;
- **keep one foot in the black**: stay on the already burned side, which can't flare up again;
- smother the flames with a leafy green branch, a shovel, a blanket, a wet sack, or throw earth with a shovel;
- **if the flames go above your knees, or the fire moves faster than you walk, you're no longer putting it out: you're leaving.**

### 3. The fire is coming towards your house

**In France, the official advice is clear: a solid house with cleared surroundings is the best shelter. Don't leave on the road at the last minute.** If you're going to leave, leave early, before the smoke is on you, or when the authorities tell you to. (Some countries, like Australia, advise leaving early in most cases: follow your local guidance.)

If you stay:

1. **Open the gate** for the firefighters. Put cars away, or park them in a cleared area.
2. **Bring in anything that burns**: garden furniture, cushions, umbrellas, firewood, jerrycans. Move gas bottles away from the house.
3. **Close everything**: shutters, windows, doors, hatches. **Block vents and the bottoms of doors with wet towels.**
4. **Fill** baths, buckets, bins: water for afterwards. The mains may cut out.
5. **Dress in cotton or wool**, long sleeves, closed shoes. No synthetics, which melt onto skin.
6. **When the front passes, stay inside**, away from windows, in a room on the far side. It's very hot, it's loud, it lasts a few minutes. **Walls block the radiant heat that kills outdoors.**
7. **As soon as it has passed, go out and walk round**: embers on the roof, in the gutters, under the deck, in the hedges. **Most houses burn after the front has passed, because of embers.** That's the moment your water and your shovel save the house.

### 4. You're in a car

- **Don't drive into smoke.** Turn back while you can still see.
- If the fire catches you: park **on ground without vegetation** (car park, ploughed field, wide verge), **headlights on**, windows and vents shut.
- **Stay in the car**, lying below window level, under a wool or cotton blanket. The car won't explode. It will be very hot for a few minutes.
- Get out once the front has passed, and move into the burned area.

### 5. You're on foot

- **Never flee uphill**: fire climbs faster than you.
- Go **to the side** of the fire's direction, towards an **already burned area**, a wide road, a ploughed field, a body of water, a scree slope.
- **Avoid gullies, ravines and saddles**: fire speeds up there like in a chimney.
- Trapped: **lie down in a hollow or behind a rock**, face to the ground, cover yourself with earth or a wool blanket, protect your nose and mouth with a cotton cloth, damp if you have water.

## ADAPT

**The wind shifts.** A calm flank becomes a fire head within minutes. Keep reassessing your way out, especially in the early afternoon.

**There's smoke but no visible flame.** Smoke travels far and fast. Close everything, wear a filtering mask if you have one, and listen to local radio to find out where the fire is. See [[URG-AIR-001]].

**Animals.** Open enclosures and field gates: a free animal escapes better than a shut-in one. Bring dogs and cats into the house with you.

**Children, elderly people.** Leave early with them, at the first warning. You don't evacuate a vulnerable person through smoke.

**Burns.** Cool with lukewarm water for twenty minutes, see [[URG-BRUL-001]].

**Afterwards.** Don't go into a burned area without permission: falling trees, smouldering stumps, ground collapsing over burned-out roots. And watch for hot spots at home for 48 hours.

## UNDERSTAND

**What kills in a wildfire is first of all radiant heat.** It burns tens of metres from the flames, through the air. Anything that makes a screen, a wall, a car body, a rock, a bank of earth, cuts that radiation dramatically. Hence the rule: **shelter behind something solid rather than run in the open.**

**The front passes quickly.** At any given spot, the big flames only last a few minutes, a little longer in dense forest. Holding out behind shelter for that time is enough to survive in the vast majority of cases.

**Most victims die on the road**, fleeing too late, in smoke where they can no longer see. Hence the other rule: **leave early, or don't leave.**

**A house with cleared surroundings holds**: with no continuous vegetation up to the walls, the fire passes by and leaves only embers to put out. That's why clearing around houses is compulsory in at-risk areas. The full phenomenon is described in [[TEC-TER-001]], and firefighters' work in [[TEC-TER-002]].

fiches.corps:
::A Canadair doesn't put out a wildfire. It slows a fire head so crews on the ground can hold it. A wildfire is won on the ground, with hoses, shovels and bulldozers, often at night.::

## The French doctrine: hit fast

France's strategy rests on the **massive attack on new fires**: during the risk season, resources are pre-positioned and aircraft patrol loaded with water, to hit every new fire within minutes. **The vast majority of fires are stopped this way before they cover a single hectare.** A fire that escapes that first attack, on the other hand, can last for days.

## Who responds

- **Firefighters** from the departmental fire services, in wildland fire tenders, grouped into columns.
- **Civil Security military units**, specialised in large fires and reinforcements.
- **Foresters**, who know the ground, the tracks and the water points.
- **Air assets**: **Canadairs**, which scoop about 6 tonnes of water in a dozen seconds skimming the sea or a lake, **Dash 8** aircraft, which drop a red retardant, and water-bombing helicopters.

## Direct attack

When the fire is still small or calm, it's attacked **on its edge**, where the flames meet the vegetation: water from hoses, fire beaters, shovels, thrown earth. **Always starting from a safe point**, a road, a rock, an already burned area, called **the anchor point**, and working up the **flanks** towards the head. A violent fire head is never attacked from the front.

## Indirect attack

When the fire is too strong, crews work **ahead of it**, at a distance:

- **The control line**: a strip where all fuel is removed down to bare soil, by bulldozer or hand tools, tied into a road or track.
- **Retardant** dropped from the air: a product based on ammonium salts that soaks the vegetation and slows burning, even after the water has evaporated.
- **Tactical fire**, or backfire: deliberately lighting, from a control line, a fire that burns the vegetation **towards** the wildfire. When the front arrives, it finds nothing left to burn. A powerful and dangerous technique, reserved for trained personnel and precise wind conditions.

## Night and mop-up

- **At night the fire calms down**: the air cools and grows damper, the wind often drops. That's when ground crews gain the most ground, while aircraft aren't flying.
- **A contained fire isn't out.** The edge must be **mopped up**: digging, turning, soaking every stump and root that smokes, tens of metres inside the burned area. A poorly mopped-up fire restarts the next day with the afternoon wind.

## Crew safety

Wildland firefighters all over the world apply the same rule, summed up in the United States by the acronym **LACES**:

- **Lookouts**: people watching how the fire develops;
- **Anchor points**: a safe anchor;
- **Communications**: a radio that works;
- **Escape routes**: escape routes scouted in advance;
- **Safety zones**: safe areas to shelter in, often an already burned area.

The oldest rule of ground crews fits in one image: **keep one foot in the black**, meaning stay at the edge of the already burned area, where the fire can't come back.

## What the old hands know

- **Fire changes in the early afternoon**: the hottest, driest, often windiest hour. Many tragedies happen between 2 and 5 pm.
- **A sudden lull is suspicious**: the wind can shift and turn a quiet flank into a fire head.
- **Narrow gullies, steep ravines and saddles** act like chimneys: fire speeds up violently there. Never go into one above a fire.
- **Aircraft don't fly at night or in thick smoke**, and wind that's too strong grounds them: the most dangerous days are often the ones where they help least.

For the phenomenon itself: [[TEC-TER-001]]. For what a private person can do: [[URG-FEU-001]].
